If you want the extra ball you have to keep one eye on the screen and one on the grid, which is why a machine with dead Matrix lamps is a genuinely worse machine to play.

items: **Light Extra Ball** and **Light Crazy Bob's** (a power item and 200 million) are the two awards worth breaking your plan for.
**Super Loops** makes both loops worth 25 million for the rest of the ball, and 50 million if you collect it again later in the game.
**Bonus X**, **Hold Bonus**, **Award Bonus** and **50 GB** are rarely worth redirecting for.
**Mystery** is a wildcard: it can start Yakuza Strike, light the outlane Special or drop you into Touch-Tone Multiball.
Drop the ball off the Matrix and the locks simply relight — you lose nothing but time.

body.text: Lock in a straight line

Three balls locked in a row triple every jackpot for the whole multiball. Since you are steering the glove anyway, this costs nothing but planning — decide on your line before the first drop, because correcting later wastes a lock. Your column also picks your jackpot shots: left gives the left jet lane, spinner lane and left loop; the middle gives the middle jet lane and both ramps; the right gives the right jet lane, right loop and Crazy Bob's. A tripled jackpot on a shot you keep bricking is worth less than a single on one you own.
Yakuza Strike is the big number

Each ramp carries three red triangles, and hitting each ramp three times lights all six and starts Yakuza Strike. A timer opens at 60 million and drops about a million per second, and every lit shot pays whatever is left. Crucially it bottoms out at 25 million rather than zero, so there is no such thing as a wasted late shot. It also runs during multiball. If you can light the sixth ramp and immediately lock your third ball, the two stack and the numbers get silly.
The inlane awards you should be using

The left inlane lights Throwing Spears, collected at the right ramp or right loop. The awards come in a fixed order and reset when you drain: gigabytes, points, Lite Spinner, Quick Multiball, Hold Bonus, extra ball. Quick Multiball alone is worth working toward: a second ball launches and both ramps pay 50 million jackpots while you keep them alive. The right inlane lights Hit Me for one quick shot at the left loop, worth 25 million then 45 million. Given a choice, Spears usually wins.
Modes, and the road to Power Down

The centre lane is lit for Start Mode from the moment the game begins. The selected mode rotates every couple of seconds, so you pick by timing the shot. Every mode opens with 30 million banked, and every made shot resets the timer to fifteen seconds if it had fallen below — which makes completion far more achievable than it first looks.

items: **Upload** — both ramps and both loops, any order, 50/70/90/110 million.
**Cartoon Hero** — the same shots and the same ladder, but in a fixed order that makes you cross the playfield each time.
**Riot** — a bumper mode. Bumpers pay eight million, and completing the top lanes multiplies the bumper value as well as the bonus.
**Download** — three left loops for 60, 90 and 120 million.
**N.A.S. Cure** — four centre lane shots for 60 up to 150 million. The best payout and the hardest shot.

body.text: Finish any mode and Crazy Bob's lights up: a power item plus 200 million. Collect them. Play all five modes and Power Down opens: all four balls in play, every white triangle shot worth 400 million, and the playfield going dark section by section as the game powers down around you. With no power items banked the whole thing is over in about half a minute. With them, you get room to work.

One last piece of housekeeping. Mnemonic Recovery is a left-outlane ball save that starts the game lit, and relighting it takes two hits on the right standup — the first does nothing while Recovery is still on. The returned ball is not diverted, so it arrives out of the left loop at speed. Be ready instead of watching the display.

name: Jokerz!
description: A player's guide to Williams' Jokerz!: the gate cycle that drives the whole game, filling poker hands on the upper level, the ramp award, and the last-ball score double.

body.text: Jokerz is a late-eighties Williams with a short rule set and one shot that does almost everything. A raised upper level at the back holds five card lanes; below it sit three banks of drop targets, two side ramps, a raisable centre ramp and a draw poker saucer that spins a wheel in the backglass. It is not a deep game, but it rewards a player who picks one plan and repeats it.
The layout

items: **Upper level card lanes** — five rollovers, Ace on the left through to the ten. Rolling one lights that card, and the flipper buttons shift lit lanes across.
**The gate** — above the upper left drop targets. Lights the lowest unlit card and ejects the ball into the B-E-T rollovers.
**B-E-T rollovers** — advance the bonus multiplier, with three pop bumpers underneath keeping the ball rattling back over them.
**Left and right ramps** — the left builds the ramp award, the right collects it. Both climb to the upper level.
**Centre ramp and target** — the ramp only exists once the target has raised it. This is the lock and jackpot shot.
**Draw poker saucer** — under the upper level beside the right ramp, lit by the left inlane. Spins the backglass wheel.
**Three drop banks** — lower left, lower right and upper left, three targets each.

body.text: The gate is the game

One shot advances four things at once. Shooting the gate lights the lowest card you do not yet have, then ejects the ball into the B-E-T rollover area, where the pop bumpers knock it back through the rollovers repeatedly and build your bonus multiplier for free. A fair proportion of the time the ball comes back out through the gate on its own, and the cycle starts again. The upper left drop bank also tends to clear itself while you work the shot — one third of the Millions qualifier for free. It is comfortable from the right flipper and an easy backhand from the left, and low risk in a game where several other shots are not.
Filling hands

Light all five upper level cards and the game pays a hundred thousand plus your current bonus. Because the payout includes the bonus, when you complete a hand matters as much as whether you do. Finishing two hands on one ball with a maxed multiplier is the single biggest score the machine offers, since you then collect the bonus again at the end of the ball. Completed hands are counted by the lit bells in the joker's hat, and finishing the set — three by default, though operators can raise it — lights a Special in the draw poker saucer. That saucer is a left-flipper shot and effectively cannot be backhanded.
Ramps, locks and the centre target

The side ramps are a build-and-cash pair. Each left ramp shot raises the award through roughly ten, twenty five, fifty, a hundred, two hundred and fifty and five hundred thousand at the ceiling. The right ramp collects the lot and drops the value back to the bottom, so only cash when it is worth the risk. Both share a hazard: a ball that trips the top switch then rolls back down comes out between the flippers, so keep a slap save ready. The centre target is worse. Hit dead centre from a trapped ball it returns straight down the middle, and off-line it kicks off a post rubber into an outlane. The safe version is to flip at a live ball already rolling down the inlane at an angle, which bounces the target and sends the ball back into play.
Multiball and the jackpot

items: Raise the centre ramp with the centre target, lock a ball, raise it again, lock the second. Multiball is two balls only.
The jackpot needs four centre ramp shots during multiball and builds toward a four million ceiling. Progress may carry to a later multiball depending on the settings.
Flip one ball up through the gate and let it live in the bumpers, then work the ramp with the other. Trying to control both at once usually costs you one of them straight away.
The target behind the gate doubles playfield values for twenty seconds during multiball — take it early so the window covers your ramp shots.
Clearing all three drop banks starts a timed Millions round where each bank you complete pays a million.

body.text: A plan that works

There are two ways to an extra ball. The reliable one is the bonus multiplier: push it to the flashing value and the light comes on over the in and outlanes. It only works once per ball, but the multiplier carries over, so each ball starts closer than the last. The other is the draw poker wheel, which is luck. So the plan is simple — grind the gate every ball until the extra ball lights, take it, and only risk the centre target once you have that cushion. Save the score double for your genuine last ball. It gives you one window to double everything by hitting both side ramps, the window shrinks by five seconds for every million you already have down to a floor of ten, and progress does not carry onto an extra ball. If you have one lit on ball three, score first, collect it, and make the attempt on the extra ball instead.

name: Last Action Hero
description: A guide to Last Action Hero: the Dynamite Feature list, M-Ball and 6 Ball, the title round, World Premier, Second Cousin Frank's, and where to spend your Smart Missile.

body.text: Last Action Hero looks like a shot-collecting game and is really a completion game. The lights above the flippers are a checklist of Dynamite Features, the movie scoop hands you whichever is flashing, and the pop bumpers change which one that is. Finishing a round adds five million to the World Premier award, so completions compound into the ending.
How the features cycle

items: The scoop starts each ball lit. Spend it and the ramp relights it; an inlane relights it for a **very** short window.
Steady lights are finished rounds. The flashing light is what the scoop will give you next.
The **left captive ball resets the current round's timer to full**, once per round. Save it for a good Blow Out.
An inlane lights the Wildcard scoop during most rounds. Taking it there **doubles that round's scoring**.
Most rounds stack. Go to the Movies, Super Crane and multiball are the ones that lock everything else out.

body.text: Which rounds are worth your time

The Roof is the most repeatable: three ramps in twenty seconds for thirty million, and each made ramp diverts to the right inlane so the next shot is set up for you. Red Eye is three eyeball targets for the same total. Big Mistake crosses the playfield twice in a fixed order — CRANE target, eyeball, movie scoop.

Blow Out is the frenzy round: twenty seconds on a six million base, switches worth 250K climbing 50K every ten hits toward a one million ceiling. The Lt. Dekker spinner drops the ball straight into the bumpers, the fastest way to feed it. A typical round is twenty million; a ball that lives in the pops can push thirty.

Two rounds are not worth chasing. Go to the Movies pays poorly, blocks everything else, and its captive hits do not advance multiball. Find Benedict hides him in one of three scoops at random and pays nothing for a wrong guess.
Locking, M-Ball and 6 Ball

Clearing all five CRANE drop targets starts Runaway Crane, a hurry-up from ten million down to three, and lights the crane lock whether or not you collect it. Watch the Danger Bar behind the bank — hitting it stands every target back up. Two balls is the maximum, and clearing the bank with two already locked pays seven million.

Captive ball hits light M-Ball at the movie scoop, and an inlane first doubles the credit each hit gives you. Lock before you start: the jackpot is fifteen million plus five per locked ball, capped at twenty-five. The ramp collects it, and the crane pays **double** inside ten seconds. That double jackpot is what starts 6 Ball.

6 Ball runs a loop. Collect the four 5M badges — left captive ball, crane, Ripper, Wildcard scoop — then the crane for thirty million, the badges again, the ramp for a super jackpot of fifty million per ball in play, then the crane for double that. Keeping balls alive matters more than any single shot, because every drain cuts the super jackpot.
The title round is the big one

Three Dynamite Features are the words of the title, worth ten million each at the movie scoop. You need not wait for them: the Wildcard scoop forces the next feature to the next unlit word, so you can drive straight at it — scoop, ramp to relight, scoop, ramp, scoop.

Completing it puts six balls out with twenty-five seconds and asks for fifty target hits. Make them and you take the running award, gain time, and are asked for fifty more. Feed the spinner into the bumpers and this can last minutes. If you will not make the count, burn the Smart Missile. One warning: if the timer climbs past ninety-nine seconds it wraps to zero and the round ends.
World Premier, and the award that hides

Clear every feature, title round included, and the movie scoop starts World Premier. You take a flat award, then the scoop pays a million per seated patron until the theatre fills — and the number of seats depends on how many rounds you completed earlier.

Second Cousin Frank's is the hidden treasure. It grows between games until somebody collects it, fed by ramp shots and by balls returning to the chicken scoop through the bumper lane. To take it: two consecutive ramps, then the chicken scoop, with the ball touching nothing in between.
Combos, rescues and the missile

items: **Crane, ramp, ramp, right captive ball** — ten million and four advances toward M-Ball in one string.
**Crane, ramp, ramp, Ripper** — ten million and three RIPPER letters.
**Five ramp-ramp pairs** turn the Dekker spinner from 50K a spin into a million a spin on your next shot.
The RIPPER bounty is held across balls, players and whole games — check what it is worth before chasing it.
Balls come back generously: after CRANE target hits, shortly after a Ripper shot, and on the plunge. A ball nudged back in from an outlane pays three million.

body.text: You get one Smart Missile per ball, it is awkwardly placed, and an outlane drain kills it. It pays whatever is lit. The best use is 6 Ball: take the first badge set yourself, the crane for thirty million, then press it to light the ramp for a super jackpot. It will not hand you a flashing feature — it lights multiball at the scoop instead.

name: Mario Andretti
description: A guide to Mario Andretti: the captive ball skill shot, running laps on fuel, Checkered Flag choices, the Stop Watch, jackpot building, and the World Championship.

body.text: Mario Andretti is a narrow-body racing game with one objective buried under a lot of noise: win three races in first place and you reach the World Championship. Everything else either drives your car around the track or makes the finishing awards bigger. Play it as a race and it makes sense.
The plunge is a real decision

Your plunged ball strikes a captive ball, which climbs a path over three switches into a standup at the top. Whichever switch it last touched decides your award, so plunge strength is everything. Soft gives Jackpot, medium gives Lock Ball and starts regular multiball, hard gives Race Strategy, and full force sends it into the standup for a token score and a gallon of fuel. Once you take an award it is off the menu until you have collected the others.
Laps, fuel and finishing position

Seventeen numbered car lights form the circuit. Lit yellow shots move your car, and so do the spinning cars, the slingshots and the pop bumpers — the cars spin faster as your lap progresses, which is your speedometer. The first race is one lap; every race after is two.

items: You start with **five gallons** and burn one per lap. Empty means your car stops moving no matter what you shoot.
The right hole is the pit lane. Shoot it when Pit In is lit for **three gallons**.
Fuel is money — the game pays **ten million a gallon** at the end, so never finish with a dry tank.
Track Awards, Mystery, the Pass/Yield Round and a three-to-four-second Stop Watch all hand out fuel too.

body.text: You start every race in first place and the playfield spends the lap trying to take it off you. Green shots pass a car; red shots are a Yield and drop you a position. While you are leading, a green shot instead adds five million to the pass bonus, which is what the end-of-ball bonus pays. Finishing first is fifty million and lights the extra ball standup; second is thirty, third is ten, fourth or worse is nothing. Only a win counts as a Victory Circle.
Checkered Flag: pick a lane

Every finished race offers two awards, one on each flipper button, and the two sides advance independently. Turn one down and it comes back next time. The left side runs Redline Round, Race Strategy, Super Jackpot, Spin Cars Round; the right side runs Multiball, Pass/Yield Round, five jackpots, Multiball. When a side reads Complete you have taken everything on it, and choosing it gives you the other side's award instead.

The Spin Cars Round is the one to steer toward. Two opening skill shots — the first awards Race Strategy, and doubled jackpots for the rest of the ball if you have not had it — then a three-ball round where every rotation of the cars is a jackpot. Feed either mouth of the hairpin and let the ball rattle. The Redline Round is the opposite: five worthless Tach hits buy fifty million a hit afterward, but the moment the Tach lights for fifty, the up post and **both** outlane saves switch off.
Build before you cash

Jackpots start at thirty million and super jackpots at two hundred, and both are worth raising first. A hairpin shot sets the Tach flashing; hit the Tach before it stops and the jackpot climbs five million. The super jackpot climbs a hundred million from a fast Stop Watch, and from certain Track Awards.

The Stop Watch is a two-shot puzzle. Light it at the left ramp, shoot the right loop to start a timer counting up, then shoot the loop again to stop it — touch nothing else in between or the round dies. The loop returns to the left inlane, so trap and fire immediately. Under three seconds pays the super jackpot advance; three to four gives three gallons; four to seven gives one. Beat the machine's record and it stops the game there and then to take your initials, and awards a free one.
Multiball carries over

Regular multiball walks a ladder: both sides of the hairpin and the right loop for ten million each, then those three relight at twenty with the Tach added, then the right hole joins for the jackpot tier, then the left ramp for a Super Jackpot. Where you stopped carries into your next multiball. The exception is the Super Jackpot — collect one and the next multiball starts you back at the bottom.
The ball saves are a see-saw

This is the detail that catches everyone. The left slingshot arms the right outlane diverter and disarms the left kickback; the right slingshot does exactly the reverse. You are almost never covered on both sides at once, and the ball keeps flipping which side is safe. Everything is enabled for a long spell at the start of each ball, and a right loop briefly raises the up post after that. There is also guaranteed ball time — a third ball that ends too quickly is handed back.
The championship

Three Victory Circles opens the World Championship: two skill shots at the top rollover, then a three-ball round where every major shot advances cars and every completed lap pays a Super Jackpot. This is why the Stop Watch grind matters — arrive with the super jackpot built up and each lap is worth several times more.

name: Monopoly
description: A player's guide to Stern's Monopoly: rolling the dice at Roll & Collect, the eight colour group modes, all five multiballs, and how to qualify Land Grab.

body.text: Monopoly was Pat Lawlor's first design for Stern, and it is far deeper than the Stern games that came before it. The lower playfield is taken up by a lit game board turned on the diagonal, with GO sitting between the flippers. Your token moves around that board, and where it lands decides what you play. Land on a property and you collect the whole colour group and start its mode. Land on a corner and a multiball begins. Own all eight groups and all four railroads, and you get Land Grab.
The layout

items: **Water Works** — a saucer guarded by a motorised flipper that sweeps across the entrance. The skill shot, and it scores identically during normal play.
**Roll & Collect lane** — beside the Bank door. Runs the ball around the vault into the saucer, where the dice actually get rolled.
**Bank vault door** — hits on the closed door spell B-A-N-K. The centre ramp behind it is the lock shot.
**Free Parking ramp** — the upper left ramp, reachable only from the upper right flipper. Every multiball jackpot except Railroad lives here.
**Right ramp** — relights Roll & Collect, and diverts to the shooter lane to fire multiball off.
**Railroad ramp** — an open wire ramp that returns the ball just above the left flipper. Collects railroads and arms super jackpots.
**Electric Company** — a short ramp from the upper right flipper into the lower jets. Powers the meter that holds your extra ball.
**Chance scoop** — far left, for cards that range from trivial to a free multiball.
**Cop drop target** — sits in front of the Roll & Collect lane. Every hit adds five seconds to whatever mode is running.

body.text: Roll and collect

This is the loop the whole game runs on. Shoot the right ramp to light Roll & Collect, knock the Cop drop target down so it stops blocking the lane, then take the lane. The dice roll, your token walks the board, and you are paid a thousand times the printed price of whatever you land on. New York Avenue at two hundred dollars pays two hundred thousand. The rolls are quietly weighted in your favour — the game steers you toward colour groups you do not yet own, and when there is nothing in range it aims you at an unowned railroad or a corner instead.
The eight colour groups

Landing on any property in a group hands you the entire group and starts its mode, so you never need to revisit a colour twice. Light blue runs Token Race, where your car races the dog and every major shot advances you. Violet is Free Money, where each Bank door hit locks a digit of the payout on the Electric Company ticker. Orange is a hurry-up starting at half a million on the Bank door. Red is Board Chase, where Cop hits reverse your token's direction and keep it away from the Go To Jail corner. Yellow turns the jets into a scoring engine and stacks with other modes. Green pays a flat one, two or three million. Purple maxes a jet bank. Dark blue lights either an extra ball or a Special, depending on which square the dice pick — and you only get one of the two per game.
Five different multiballs

items: **Monopoly Multiball** — lap the board to light lock, lock two balls up the centre ramp, start on the right ramp. Jackpots begin at a million.
**Railroad Multiball** — collect all four railroads. The only multiball whose jackpot is on the Railroad ramp instead of Free Parking.
**Breakout** — a corner mode from landing on Just Visiting, jackpots from four hundred thousand.
**Free Parking** — the corner mode with a memory. Its jackpot equals the Free Parking value, which grows five thousand per standup hit and carries between games to a half-million ceiling.
**Ripoff** — landing on Go To Jail empties the lock and throws your banked balls into play whether you wanted them or not.

body.text: Land Grab

Own it all. All eight monopolies and all four railroads light Roll & Collect one more time, and taking it starts a timed four-ball multiball where you build property as fast as you can shoot. The centre ramp builds one house. The Free Parking ramp builds four and adds time to the clock. The Electric Company builds hotels. The right ramp moves you on to the next property. Both of the high-value shots want the upper right flipper, so getting a ball parked up there early is worth more than a fast start.
What to actually do

items: Hit the Cop target constantly. It pays up to two hundred and fifty thousand and buys five seconds of every timed mode you play.
Push the Electric Company to thirty per cent for the extra ball. That is six ramp shots on default settings.
Complete the A-B-C lanes whenever you can — they advance the bonus multiplier and move your token eight spaces at once.
Do not shoot the Chance scoop unlit; it only pays Pocket Change, which is not worth the return risk.
The Free Parking standup is worth feeding even when nothing is lit, because you are banking a better multiball for later.

name: Mustang
description: A guide to Stern's Mustang: the Super Skill Shot, climbing the gears, all six modes, Burnout and Mustang multiballs, RPM scoring and reaching Drift.

body.text: Mustang runs on two tracks at once. The gear ladder decides which multiball you get and what your super jackpot is worth. The six modes decide whether you see the game's deep end. Neither feeds the other, and most players spend a whole game on one without realising the other exists.
Start with the skill shot

Hold the left flipper in before you launch. Three lamps in front of the gears targets sweep back and forth — GE, A and RS — and hitting the A while its lamp is lit advances you two gears in one shot, though it will not carry you past gear four. GE and RS each pay a million, and the scoop pays two.

The real skill is arriving at a stationary ball, because any significant shot beforehand cancels it. Plunge somewhere you can control: softly, so it traps on the right flipper, or hard enough to catch it live on the left or pass it across the loop. Which works depends on your machine.
Climbing the gears
You start in first gear, and each completed set of drop targets shifts you up one. Gears five and six add a timing requirement on top.

items: **Gears two to four** — just clear the drop bank.
**Gear five** — clear all the drops, then hit one of the two standups behind them inside five seconds.
**Gear six** — clear the drops, hit one standup inside five seconds, then the other within another five.
The super jackpot is the **sum of the gears** you have climbed: gear four pays ten million, gear six normally pays twenty-one, but the very first gear six super is boosted to fifty million.
Once a gear's multiball has been played it is gone. Start in third and your next has to be four, five or six; start in sixth and you have to come back down.

body.text: That first super jackpot has a generous timer, and the right thing to do with it is not to shoot the super. Go and arm the N2O boost first. Double scoring on a fifty million super is the biggest single swing available to you.
The six modes

Modes are selected and started at the scoop, and there are two thresholds worth knowing. Merely starting all six prepares Drift; lighting all six solid — actually finishing them — prepares Silverball Stampede.

items: **Cruisin'** — the only mode needing two starts. The first pass wants every shot once, and taking them strictly left to right doubles each. The second wants the first four in order, then a roving light caught four times, faster each time.
**Road Course** — the first four of six lit shots advance you, then the two you skipped become the only ones that count, needing four more hits between them before the scoop ends the race.
**Police Pursuit** — cheapest of the top row at eight shots. Alternate sides for yellow light, any of four for red light, then right orbit twice and left ramp twice.
**Stunt Driver** — gears target, left ramp, then left ramp or right orbit, then anything on the right.
**Drag Race** — five standup hits pushes you to gear six and starts a multiball, completing only once you are back to single-ball play.
**Rally Race** — left, right, right, then a shortcut lights at the left ramp. Hit it and you save two shots; miss it and the captive ball becomes mandatory.

body.text: Two very different multiballs

Burnout Multiball is qualified by four hits on the captive ball, or handed to you by a Mystery Ford award after finishing one of the top three modes. It opens with three 200,000 jackpots — left ramp, captive ball, right orbit — and one lights the main jackpot at the captive ball for ten million. While you are spelling BURNOUT the left ramp diverts to the cup instead of returning to the flipper. Once the word is done the ramp feeds the flipper again, setting up a twenty million combo into the captive ball. A set number of bumper hits restarts the sequence, adding twenty million to the combo jackpot and five to the regular one each time.

Mustang Multiball is spelled out from completed modes and Mystery Ford awards, and it waits at the scoop until you want it. Four balls, every major yellow arrow lit. Collecting one shot switches all the others off and lights the shot you just made for a double jackpot; taking that double relights everything except that shot. The rhythm is new shot, same shot, new shot, same shot.
The scoring nobody expects

The three RPM standups down the right side are the most lopsided thing on the playfield. Complete them and every hit to that bank is worth two million — four with N2O running. That beats the drag race super jackpot, and it runs on a long timer you can restart by hitting the bank again. Watch the lamps: all three flash, then two, then one, then it is gone.

Two more things are easy to forget. Completing the bottom lanes and then shooting the scoop adds a ball to any multiball — set that up before you start one. And the Upgrades are a separate track: complete them once for Upgrade Scoring, twice for Upgrade Multiball. Everything funnels through that one scoop, so when awards queue up there, clear the cheapest first.

name: NBA Fastbreak
description: How NBA Fastbreak's real-basketball scoring works, the six tasks that gate Trophy Multiball, all four combos and concession modes, and why a Ring beats any score.

body.text: NBA Fastbreak keeps score like an actual basketball game. Baskets are worth two, three-pointers three, free throws one — and 300 points is an outstanding game. That one choice changes everything. There are no huge jackpots and no ladder to climb; there are six tasks, and completing all six starts Trophy Multiball, where you play for a Ring. Rings outrank points here, so a small score with a Ring beats a big score without one.
The layout

Five major shots do almost all the work, and all five are easy: **left orbit**, **left ramp**, **centre ramp**, **right ramp** and **right lane**. The centre ramp always feeds the hoop and is the shot to take from a trapped ball — miss it halfway and the ball comes straight back down the middle, the main drain in the game. The left ramp normally returns to the inlane, but a diverter can send it around to the basket instead. The right lane is your route to the bumpers, which matters more than it looks.

Below the hoop sits an arc of four numbered saucers. Land in one and it fires the ball up a wireform into the basket. That leads to the game's most generous rule: make the left or centre ramp but miss the hoop and the ball usually drops into a saucer, which shoots it in for you and awards whatever you were shooting for, plus that saucer's number. Weak shots are rarely wasted here.
The six tasks

items: **Goals** — one two-pointer, one three-pointer, one free throw. The basket is lit for a free throw whenever nothing else is lit on it.
**20 Points** — reach twenty. Spotted after your first Trophy Multiball.

**Combos** — all four. Tip-Off is right lane into centre ramp, Slam Dunk is right ramp into left ramp, Alley-Oop is left orbit into centre ramp, Fast Break is either outer ramp into centre ramp. Two points each, and the set lights an extra ball.
**Concessions** — play all four of Crazy Bob's modes at the left saucer.
**Multiballs** — finish Shoot Around and Around The World.
**Power Hoops** — start all four bumper modes. Starting is enough; you do not have to finish them.

body.text: Where the points actually are

Crazy Bob's concessions run in a fixed order and they are the scoring heart of the game. **Pizza** hands you control of a real flipper on the backglass for about ten seconds; the backglass hoop cycles between 1, 2 and 3 points, and timing your shots to land on 3 can be worth eighteen points on its own. **Hot Dog** sets a 24-second shot clock — roughly ten seconds — where any major shot is 3 points and resets the clock, though the resets get shorter until it strangles itself. **NBA Trivia** asks a basketball question: right answer 10 points, wrong answer 1, and since no shot is required you should cradle the ball and read carefully. **Egyptian Soda** pays 3 points on the outer ramps for about fifteen seconds and is the weakest of the four — letting it time out still completes the task.

Shoot Around Multiball comes from spelling S-H-O-O-T across the five major shots. Inside the two-ball multiball, spelling it a second time lights an extra ball, and that is the reason to play it. Around The World needs all four saucer numbers, mostly collected through In The Paint: roll an inlane, the opposite orbit or lane lights for about ten seconds, and shooting it drops you into a saucer where a plastic guard slides toward you. Pass between saucers with the flippers until you are clear, then shoot the hoop with the button. Once the three-ball multiball starts, ignore the flashing shot — it only pays a point per ball in play — and shoot free throws instead.
Power Hoops, the awkward task

Power Hoops modes start on bumper hits alone, commonly at 11, 22, 33 and 44, though this varies and the machine lowers the requirement if you keep coming up short. Three of the four light a single ramp for 3 points — Half Court on the centre ramp, Hook Shot on the left, Run & Shoot alternating between them — and the fourth is a two-ball mode. On a machine with dead bumpers this is by far the slowest task. Your hits come mostly from the right lane, plus whatever the basket kicks back down toward the bumpers.
Extra balls and the last-ball gamble

None of the extra balls are random, which is unusual and welcome. All light at the left saucer and they stack without limit: all four combos lights one, a second S-H-O-O-T lights one, ten free throws lights one (some machines are set as low as three, and this route works once a game), and a long grind of left orbit loop combos lights another. Free throws during Around The World are the cheapest route.

On your last ball — or after your final extra ball — the right outlane lights for the Million Dollar Shot. Draining there on purpose launches another ball with about ten seconds to make the basket from the centre ramp. There is no compensation here: hit the ramp and miss the hoop and it does not count. Make it and your game carries on. And since this game has no end-of-ball bonus at all, tilting away a lost ball costs you nothing.

name: Popeye Saves the Earth
description: How to play Popeye Saves the Earth: the skill wheel, doubling Round House loops, Spinach Cans, Bluto Multiball, the upper Kneedeep playfield and the Rescue Olive wizard mode.

body.text: Popeye Saves the Earth is a cluttered widebody with short flippers, a wide centre drain, and several shots you cannot see clearly from where you stand. But there is a clean route through it, and knowing that route is the difference between a two-minute ball and a real game.
Two playfields

Downstairs: **P-O-P** standups left and **E-Y-E** right, a **Round House loop** each side, a **left ramp**, an **Animal sinkhole**, Bluto's head in the middle with a **jab target** either side and the **Lockjaw** hole as his mouth, pop bumpers behind him, the **O-Y-L rollovers** above those, a **Fight Bluto** sinkhole, and the **Escalator**. **SEA** and **HAG** targets sit on opposite sides.

Upstairs splits in two: the **Animals** section, fed by the Animal sinkhole, and **Kneedeep**, a mini-playfield reachable only via the Escalator, holding the Swea' Pea gates, the Super Animal exit and the **2X Wheel**. A rotating **skill wheel** on the right takes the plunge and empties into the right inlane.
Start at the wheel

The plunge lands on a disc carrying eight awards in fixed order: 100K, 10M, Light Lock, Spinach Can, OYL, Spot Animal, 2M and Spot Item. **Light Lock is the one to want.** Take it, shoot Lockjaw, and Bluto Multiball can be three shots from the start of a ball — the shortest route to points here. Many of these machines have a weak plunger and a stopper on the launch rail that bounces the ball back, so the shot is not always controllable.
Loops and the ramp

The **Round House loops** are the biggest repeatable score downstairs. A lit loop pays 2M and each consecutive lit loop doubles it — 2M, 4M, 8M, 16M, 32M. Consecutive is literal: hit any other switch in between and you are back to 2M. Only one inlane is lit for Light Loop at a time, and **the lit side swaps every time you press a flipper**, so check before you commit. Right inlane lights the left loop and vice versa.

The **left ramp** is the quiet workhorse. Its counter pays out every fourth shot — four lights a Spinach Can, eight lights the extra ball, twelve another Can, sixteen spots an animal. It also feeds the right inlane, which lights the left loop. When nothing better is lit, shoot the ramp.
About that extra ball: it lights **in the left outlane**, and the only way to collect it is to drain there. Once the light is on, stop nudging away from the left side.
Spinach Cans

Five shots carry a Spinach Can — the left ramp, both loops, the Animal sinkhole and the Fight Bluto sinkhole. A lit Can **doubles the entire value of that shot**, jackpots included, and stays lit for the rest of the ball or until you use it. Spelling POPEYE lights one, as do the ramp counter, the Escalator and the wheel. The first is always the left ramp — convenient, because a Can there doubles a jackpot.
Multiballs

items: **Bluto Multiball** — hit both jab targets to light Lockjaw, lock three. Jackpots are 30M times the jackpot number, collected on the left ramp and relit at Lockjaw, capped at 180M even doubled. Drain to one ball with nothing collected and you get about twenty seconds to restart at Lockjaw.

**Sea Hag Multiball** — collect four Items from the left ramp lit by the SEA and HAG targets, then the Animal sinkhole starts a four-ball instant multiball. Return each item at a different shot: a POPEYE target, an OYL rollover, a Swea' Pea gate and the 2X Wheel.
**Mutant Spinach Multiball** — five balls, after four Fight Bluto wins in one game.

body.text: Upstairs, and what to skip

On the **Animals** section, use the left flipper kicker to push the ball out of the left lane into the animal lane. Each animal is 5M and opens a short window to save it with a loop — and it drops you into the left inlane, which lights the right loop for exactly that save. Save all five and a hurry-up around 50M starts at the left ramp.

On **Kneedeep**, hit the two standups to light Super Animal, then take either Super Animal (a double-value animal) or the **2X Wheel** exit, which collects the extra ball when lit and doubles whatever the wheel lands on next. Hunting Swea' Pea behind the three gates is only worth it if you are chasing the wizard mode — narrow gaps, heavy rubber, and almost no feedback when you find him.
Fights, and the end of the game

Completing O-Y-L adds a bonus multiplier and lights the **Fight Bluto** sinkhole. The four rounds have no clock — you win or he does. Earth Pavers is a wall race to fifteen blocks and every pop bumper hit smashes one, so feed the bumpers. Never Green Logging is a race to six trees, Blutonium Waste a race over six barrels and the toughest of the four, and Spill Oil Co. a tug of war. Lit loops count towards winning, and the timer runs on while the ball is out of play.

**Rescue Olive** is the wizard mode, and the checklist is brutal: Sea Hag Multiball, all five animals, Bluto Multiball, Swea' Pea and all four fights, in one game. Only then does the six-ball round start — and you still have to light all five Spinach Cans and shoot Lockjaw for the Super Jackpot.

name: Revenge from Mars
description: A guide to Revenge from Mars: how the nine modes flow without a start button, collecting all nine saucer lights, every multiball, and the road to Attack Mars.

body.text: Revenge from Mars looks strange at first, because half the playfield is a projected video image and the targets you shoot live behind it. Look at the machine while the projector is idle and note where the centre target bank and the flat mini ramp actually sit. After that it reads like any other Williams game of the era, and a generous one — extra balls replace replays by default, so a good game runs a long time.
There is no start-mode shot

This is what confuses new players. A mode is always running. Nine of them split into three groups — Fuel, Weapons and a middle Saucer group — and you pick your starting group with the curved action buttons around the flipper buttons. Take too long and the machine picks for you. Finish a mode and the next one in that group starts immediately. The Saucer group only unlocks once the other two are done, and an unfinished mode waits for you across a drain.

Nearly every mode ends the same way. Do enough damage and the flat mini ramp in the middle of the playfield rises with a red light on it, and one shot across it flings the ball onto a shelf while the finishing animation plays. Learn that shot early — it closes modes, Martian Attack, Bonus Wave, Mothership and the wizard mode.
Flawless, and the nine saucer lights

Finishing a mode is not the same as acing one. Do exactly what the screen asked and you get a **Flawless** rating, worth one of nine saucer lights painted at the centre of the playfield. Finish any other way and it still ends, just without the light. In Martian Happy Hour, blowing up all three kegs ends the mode instantly and costs you the light if martians are still standing.
You do not have to ace all nine modes. Four other routes exist, and mixing them is faster:

items: A Super Jackpot in Capture Multiball is worth one light.
The 15-item Bonus Wave award is a light on default settings.
Martian Multiball pays a light at ten martians destroyed and another higher up, both operator adjustable.
Stroke of Luck has one in its award pool.

body.text: Missiles are the quiet scoring engine

While a mode runs, the orbits and ramps hand out missiles, and missiles do damage inside whatever mode you are playing — so a red circle on a shot you already made is never wasted. Your first missile of a ball is 500,000 and each one after adds 100,000, so twelve deep into a long ball you are collecting over a million a shot. The value resets each ball, which argues for building it inside one good ball. Twenty missiles lights an extra ball at the scoop, thirty pays five million, and fifty lights another.
The skill shot worth taking

The plain skill shot rolls the launched ball into the lit top lane for 500,000, climbing 100,000 each time. The **Super Skill Shot** is better: hold the left flipper button while you launch, the ball skips the lanes and lands on your left flipper under control, and any ramp or orbit inside roughly ten seconds pays a million plus 200,000 on every repeat — and spots three missiles free.
Four multiballs, all different

items: **Capture Multiball** — the capture lane alternates between lighting Capture and taking one, so each lock costs two shots. Three Captures gives three balls and a shooting gallery: ten saucers at 500,000 to 1.5 million, then five hits on a big one for the Super Jackpot and a saucer light.

**Martian Multiball** — the payoff for clearing all seven martian targets and finishing Martian Attack. Two balls, every shot kills a martian for a million. Centre twice raises the mini ramp; two ramp shots kill the big martian for two million and another replaces it.

**Bonus Wave** — a four-ball round after each mode group, built around a floating 2X you push between the centre, both ramps and the lock. Cover all four and it promotes to 3X with every position free again, up to 5X. Items accumulate across the game, not per round.

**Mothership Multiball** — at forty accumulated Bonus Wave items the flippers go dead and every ball drains into it. Ramps and orbits do more damage than the centre, and killing one mothership just summons a bigger one.

body.text: Hypno Multiball

Not on any instruction card. It appears in the Stroke of Luck pool after two or three awards or several completed modes. The playfield goes dark and a large spiral appears with a beam integrity percentage. The centre targets grind it down over roughly fifteen hits while the smaller spirals add balls and short ball saves, then the mini ramp finishes it. First completion is an extra ball; the second is fifteen million.
Attack Mars

Four requirements: all nine saucer lights, all three Bonus Wave multiballs, and Mothership Multiball. The centre shot then starts a three-stage assault worth over a hundred million on the final shot alone, and unlike some wizard modes the balls do not drain between stages. The real difficulty is steering with the action buttons while still flipping — three ships lined up and shot in the middle, four targets steered to their destinations, then the Big Brain. Practise the buttons during ordinary modes so it is not a new skill when it counts.

name: Road Show
description: How to play Pat Lawlor's Road Show: mileage and the eighteen city modes, Blast multipliers, the Wheel, souvenirs, Payday Multiball and the Super Payday wizard bonus.

body.text: Road Show is a four-flipper widebody with two talking heads, eighteen modes, a shaker motor and a second plunger halfway up the left side. It is Pat Lawlor recycling his own best ideas, and there is almost always something lit somewhere. Scoring well is not about learning eighteen modes. It is about the four systems underneath them: miles, Blasts, the Wheel and souvenirs.
Miles move you west

Eighteen cities run east to west across the map, and each is a mode you start at the Start City Scene scoop or the Blast Hole. After finishing one you have to travel 400 miles to relight the scoop. The Left Loop pays 150 miles, both ramps 100, the Center Loop and both holes 75, the Lock 50, inlanes 25 and the spinner 5 a spin. The best mileage shot in the game is the Right Ramp with **Bridge Out** lit, because the diverter sends the ball round into the Left Loop and pays for both — 275 miles from one shot. The flashing city is always one of the next two on the map, and you change which one by hitting a bumper or standup of that city's colour.
Blasts and the multiplier combos

The Blast Value starts at 1M and every bumper hit adds 208,430 to it, up to 10M. Hitting the Blast Hole or the Magic Standup lights the Blast Targets for a plain collect, but how you light them decides the multiplier.

items: **Left Loop then Blast Targets** pays double the Blast Value.
**Right Ramp with Bridge Out then Blast Targets** pays triple, and advances your bonus multiplier on the way through.
**Big Blast** from the Wheel makes the targets worth five times the value — the flasher in front of them tells you when it is lit.
**Left Loop or Bridge Out into the Blast Hole** instead is a Super Blast, worth 5M, then 10M, then 15M, and it collects everything else lit at the hole at the same time.
Blasts also work as a counter: three lights Flying Rocks, and further counts hand out extra balls, Specials and more Rocks all the way up past eighty.

body.text: The Wheel and Bridge Out

Bridge Out is cross-lit by the inlanes — left inlane lights the Right Ramp, inside right inlane lights the Left Ramp. Each collect advances your bonus multiplier from 2X to 6X, then lights an extra ball, then pays 10M. Advancing the multiplier also lights the twelve-award Wheel, collected at the Lock or the Blast Hole. Bumper hits and spinner rotations step the flashing award along, so you can steer it. Worth shopping for: Jets At Max, Spinner At Max, Big Blast, a free souvenir and Light Extra Ball. One warning — if the Wheel is already lit when you push the multiplier to its maximum, the Wheel goes **out**.
Souvenirs are real points

Every Skill Shot and every Bob's Freebie hands you a free souvenir, and you can buy more with your own score at Bob's Souvenir Bunker — light it with the Center Loop or the outside right inlane, then hit the Lock with nothing else lit and no mode running. At the end of the ball, each souvenir whose matching city you have visited is worth 10M, and two of the same souvenir pays twice. Three items in Bob's stock are not souvenirs at all: the lead pinball at 75M lights an extra ball, the zinc at 100M awards one outright, and the gold at 250M gives you an extra ball plus a lit Special. And if the sign in the shop window advertises uranium ore, hit both flipper buttons quickly to start **Construction Mania** — twenty seconds with every target on the machine worth 3M.
Payday Multiball

Bulldozer blade hits advance the day of the week. Reach Friday and the Lock lights; lock two balls and Ted falls asleep, the blade lifts, and his open mouth starts multiball. The jackpot opens at 40M and every blade hit adds 5M to a 75M ceiling, and jackpots then alternate between Ted and Red. Ted's blade rises and falls when he is next, which makes his half the harder one. Two things are worth knowing. Between lighting the lock and actually locking, every blade hit pays **Overtime** — 1.1M climbing to 3M. And if you drain two balls without a single jackpot, the Lock lights for twelve seconds to restart the whole thing with two balls.
The Magic Standup and Super Payday

One standup on this machine faces the wrong way, sitting just beneath the upper left flipper's tip, and the way to hit it is to do nothing — let a ball on its way back from the Lock roll into it. It does something useful in nearly every mode in the game, once each: 16M added to the Atlanta hurry-up, two people thawed in Minneapolis, a tunnel spotted in Butte, a free Wheel award in Las Vegas, a flat 60M in Salt Lake City. Learn to leave the flipper alone. The wizard bonus, Super Payday, is reached during any of the three West Coast city modes: lock one ball in Bob's Bunker, then lock a second in the Bunker, the scoop or the Blast Hole. Everything turns on at once, and ramps and loops start paying back the points you scored in each city on the way west.

name: Roller Games
description: How to play Williams' Roller Games: arming the Magnet at the Pit, shooting the Wall, the Jetways and teams, Sudden Death, Power Plays and locking three for multiball.

body.text: Roller Games has several things to chase and none pays a fortune, so a big score comes from repeating a handful of shots rather than reaching one big round. Almost everything funnels through two features: **the Pit**, where awards are collected, and **the Wall**, where they are cashed. Learn how those relate and the rest falls into place.
The Pit feeds the Wall

The Wall is pitched almost vertical, and the upper right flipper is the one place you can shoot it from — clean chances at that flipper are rare. The Pit is the fix: an enclosed saucer behind a one-way gate, where no shot is too hard because whatever goes in stays in, and it kicks onto a habitrail delivering the ball straight to that flipper.

Better still, shoot the Pit with its Magnet lamp lit and the machine holds the ball still at the flipper tip. The mistake is universal: **do not flip early**. The countdown runs while the ball travels the rail, and flipping before it settles switches the magnet off. Wait for the call, then shoot. It is one shot only, and the Magnet is relit each ball, at the start of multiball, by Instant Lock, and by completing S-K-A-T-E.
Three arrows at the Wall

Red for Jackpot, green for Lock, orange for Million — check them before you shoot, because the same shot pays very differently depending on what is lit. There is also a useful quirk: the switch registering a Wall shot sits on the upslope, below the flat top. A ball hit just hard enough to trip it, stall and roll back over it **earns two awards from one shot**.

items: A ball that falls out the left exit or back down the entrance awards no lock, but Lock stays lit.
The game refuses to count a lock off the plunger, so a full-strength plunge up the Wall is points only.
Hitting the Wall with nothing lit banks a **Power Play**. Three lights an extra ball, eight lights the outlane Specials, and they carry all game.
Left Jetway straight into the Wall is a combo worth 100K, climbing to a 500K ceiling — and it pays on top of whatever the Wall was already giving you.

body.text: Jetways and teams

The two Jetways are the halves of the orbit, each with a spinner and a lamp. They work independently and both can be lit at once. Each inlane lights the Jetway opposite, and a full orbit lights an unlit one. You only need to **trip the spinner** to collect — so with both lit, one orbit takes both.

Every collection spots one of the six team lamps in the playfield centre, and all six lights an extra ball at the Center Lane. Two are lit free at game start, but only the first time through, and teams do not carry between balls — so this is a six-in-one-ball job. Once all six are lit, the Jetways settle at 250K each.

That Center Lane runs straight up the middle: your ball has to clear the drop targets on one side and the ramp entrance on the other, then slip past the standups with the bumpers alongside. No angle works. The consolation is that extra balls stack there and stay lit.
Roller Motion and the Scoring Cycle

With Roller Motion lit, the Pit hands out a near-random award: nothing at all, Jetter Bonus, Bonus Held, a WILLIAMS letter, Spot Team, Bonus X, Extra Ball or Lite Special. **Instant Lock** is the one to hope for — a lock and a relit Magnet at once. It is lit at game start but not each ball; the 1-2-3 standups bring it back, and since those are nearly unshootable, the bumpers do that job.

The WILLIAMS letters carry over between balls, players and games. Complete the word and a hurry-up starts at four million and falls to one, collected at the Pit. A short pause before the countdown makes the full four million possible — the trick is finishing your last letter off the S-K-A-T-E bank at the spot where the rebound drops in. Collect it and WILLIAMS resets; miss it and you lose four letters.
Multiball and Sudden Death

The W-A-R drop targets award locks in single-ball play, and three locked balls starts multiball. Expect all of them down the right inlane at once. The Magnet is armed automatically, giving one free crack at the jackpot — take it, because it is worth one and a half to four million and **every collection resets it to 1.5M**. After that the target completions are better money: S-K-A-T-E pays 100K, 150K, 200K up to a 500K cap, and W-A-R runs the same ladder.

Sudden Death starts on its own once or twice a game: fifteen seconds, every Wall shot worth a million and resetting the clock. Completing both S-K-A-T-E and W-A-R ends it with two million — but if the Wall is falling, repeats beat closing it out.
Housekeeping

items: The A-B-C standups relight the left kickback, which is unusual — it fires the ball around the orbit to the upper right flipper, so a save hands you a Wall shot.
Roller Motion is switched off during multiball; the Magnet, Jetways and Scoring Cycle keep working.
The J-E-T lanes advance the bonus multiplier to 7x. Rotate them with the flipper buttons; the orbit passes above with no gate, so aimed shots rarely land there.
S-K-A-T-E gives a WILLIAMS letter and relights the Magnet — the machine's most useful repeat task.

name: Shrek
description: How to play Stern's Shrek: the two skill shots, the Prince Charming and Swamp mode ladders, all four multiballs, and the six requirements for the Far Far Away wizard mode.

body.text: Shrek is a deep game hiding behind a licensed theme most players walk straight past. It has four separate multiballs, ten modes across two independent ladders, a fully playable mini playfield with its own ball and flippers, and a final wizard mode gated behind a six-item checklist. If you have only ever plunged and flailed at it, the machine will feel random. It is not. Almost everything on it is a counter, and once you know which shot feeds which counter the whole thing opens up.
Reading the playfield

The left side is targets: the Fiona standup, the Puss In Boots orbit that returns down the left rather than looping, the Pinocchio drop target and the four-target Baby drop bank. The centre holds the main ramp with the **Castle Guard** target standing in front of it, the three-target Shrek bank, and Prince Charming above that. The right side is where the game gets unusual — the Donkey mini playfield sits up there with the **Puss In Boots Jackpot lane** running underneath it, and the Swamp scoop and Gingy spinner feed the whole mode structure. Two captive balls spell P-I-N-B-A-L-L. Merlin, tucked by the bumpers, is your mystery award.
Start with the skill shots

There are two. The obvious one is the bottom target of the Baby bank, lit at the start of every ball, worth 500K the first time and 250K more with each one after. The one nobody finds is the Puss In Boots Jackpot lane: put the plunge through there while the skill shot is lit and you collect **double** the current value and add 250K to the next award on top. Take the secret one every time. Over a long game the difference is millions.
The two mode ladders

Prince Charming and the Swamp run in parallel, and the pop bumpers rotate both of them at once. That matters — a stray bumper hit changes what you are about to start on both ladders, so pick your target before you commit to a shot. Prince Charming is a counter target: five hits collects the flashing award, six for the next, seven after that. The Swamp is fed by the spinner, ten rotations for the first mode and five more for each one after, up to thirty.

items: **Un-Happy Hour** doubles everything you score for twenty seconds. Never take it cold — stack it on top of a multiball or a big mode.
**Dragon Multiball** is the Charming award worth chasing: two balls, six jackpot shots, and a 3M Super Jackpot if you can hold all six lit at once.
**Dinner Theater** is the best-paying Swamp mode at 6.75M for hitting all six characters inside thirty seconds.
**Ogres Are Onions** scales hard — one character pays 250K a shot, all four pays a million a shot, so spread out early and repeat later.
**Potion Problems** is the reverse: pump the Donkey targets first to raise the shot value from 300K to 750K, then cash on the ramp.

body.text: Four multiballs, four different jobs

Baby Multiball is the workhorse — clear the Baby bank three times for the first, then four, five and six. Its jackpots are priced in switch hits, so it is a bumper-and-spinner affair rather than a shot-making one. Dragon Multiball comes from Prince Charming. Donkey Multiball is the reward for completing all five characters on the mini playfield during Donkey Pinball, and it demands every character be completed twice — once up top and once down below. Its Super Jackpot is 2M, and hitting **Merlin** in the seconds immediately afterwards pays triple that. Far Far Away is the final wizard mode, and it starts on the mini playfield before spilling out onto the main one.
The Far Far Away checklist

The last mode is not a shot, it is a report card. Six boxes have to be ticked: five Castle Guard Jackpots, ten lit shots during Repay Your Debt, fifteen Baby Multiball jackpots, all five Prince Charming awards, one Donkey Multiball Super Jackpot, and 25M or more scored inside a single Swamp Wizard. Hold either flipper during play and the third instant-info screen shows exactly which of them you still owe. The Swamp Wizard requirement is the hardest, so build your game around getting there twice rather than hoping to clear 25M on your first attempt.
Habits worth building

Knock Pinocchio down early — the save post between the flippers is real protection, and the lit Tell A Lie inlane raises the target so you can re-arm it. Watch which inside inlane is lit, because the slingshots swap them constantly and a doubled spinner rip is also doubled Swamp progress. Relight Merlin with ramp shots; the game never hands you a useless mystery award. And treat the Puss In Boots and Castle Guard pair as one shot rather than two, because those jackpots are on the wizard checklist whether you were thinking about it or not.

name: South Park
description: A player's guide to South Park pinball: starting and finishing all five character modes, the three multiballs, mystery awards, and the Volcano wizard mode.

body.text: South Park is a late Sega machine built on a very simple idea and a very generous ruleset. Five characters, five shots, five modes — and three separate multiballs sitting on top of them, any one of which can swing a game by hundreds of millions. It is not a subtle machine: knowing the shots and playing for multiball beats careful flipper work, and a good night can reach a billion.
The five shots
Every mode runs through one character shot, and starting it means hitting that shot four times:

items: **Stan** is the left lane, fired straight through the pop bumpers. It is the hardest shot on the playfield and the most valuable.
**Chef** is the centre lane, which ends in a kicker that throws the ball out above the bumpers. Anything you put up the left lane gets routed through here too.
**Kenny** is the rubber figure on the right. Hit the figure or the hole behind it — both count, which makes this the most forgiving character on the machine.
**Kyle** is the ramp, which runs over the toilet and has three different exits.
**Cartman** is the deep sinkhole. A metal backboard sits behind it, so it is far more shootable than a hole that size normally is.

body.text: A character's face on the playfield flashes once you have started their mode and glows solid once you have finished it. That distinction matters more than it looks, because the two wizard modes are gated on it. Modes can be replayed whether you won them or not, but each completion raises the number of shots the next attempt costs.
The modes themselves

**Stan** is a four-ball multiball built around the bumper nest. You need three kisses, spotted either by a run of bumper hits or by another left lane shot, and each lane shot starts at 5M and grows 100K for every bumper hit you have banked. Finishing the objective does not end the scoring — keep shooting the lane until you are down to one ball.

**Chef** gives you thirty seconds to sweep all five character shots. Each pays 5M plus a million per shot already made, the last is worth 10M, and every shot buys five more seconds. Take the easy ones first and the timer will still be healthy when you get to Stan's lane. **Kyle** wants four more ramps in roughly twenty seconds for 5M, 10M, 15M and 20M — pure repeat-shot pressure. **Cartman** gives twenty seconds for three more sinkhole shots, each worth 5M plus a million for every hit you have put on the three targets above the hole, so beat those targets up first. **Kenny** is a hurry-up: four hits arm it at 10M, one more collects it.
Multiball, and why it decides the game

Five hits to the Mr. Hankey targets lights multiball at the ramp — and every further hit before you start adds 100K to the base jackpot, so there is no rush. Start it at the ramp, the toilet opens and feeds a ball to the right inlane, and you are into a five-ball affair. Hankey targets pay a 1M base jackpot and each one lights a character shot for a double. Five Hankey jackpots lights a super at the ramp worth 5M, then 10M, then another 5M on top each time after.

There is a useful quirk to remember here. While multiball is running the machine will credit you a left lane shot for shooting the Chef lane — which is the easiest Stan progress you will ever collect, given how awkward that lane is under normal conditions.
Mystery, bonus and the outlanes

The three targets above the Cartman hole light the Chef lane for a mystery award. Bonus multipliers are by far the most common result, but 7M turns up, and so does a thirty-second frenzy in which every switch on the machine pays 500K. Limp into ball three still short of 10M and the mystery can hand you a charity extra ball as well. Your end-of-ball bonus pays 100K for each hit you landed on the townsfolk targets, on the ramp or on any character shot, then multiplies the whole total — so those mystery multipliers are quietly doing real work. Both outlanes can light for special. Lighting both inlanes arms Super Fart Bumpers, which is worth doing before you start Stan's mode since that mode already pays you for bumper hits.
Two endings

Start all five modes but fail to finish at least one, and the Chef lane lights for **Spooky Vision** — a five-ball multiball where you raise each character's jackpot by hitting their own shot repeatedly. It does not appear at all if you completed all five on the first attempt.

Complete all five and the red arrow in the Chef lane and the volcano insert between the flippers both light. Shooting the Chef lane starts **Volcano**, the real wizard mode: five balls, fifteen lit character shots at 10M each. Make them all and the flippers go dead, you are handed an extra ball, and the whole thing begins again — a completed run is worth roughly 210 million. Miss the count and it simply ends when you are down to one ball.

One last thing worth knowing for the wait between games: with the machine in attract mode, pressing the flipper buttons left, left, right, right, left, left, right, right brings up the design team credits.

name: Space Station
description: A guide to Space Station: docking two balls for multiball, the Rescue Jackpot, timing Stop 'N' Score at 5x, rerolling bad target awards, and the bonus ball.

body.text: Space Station is a compact late-eighties Williams game with a shallow rule set and one genuinely good idea in the middle of it. The idea is the rotating diverter the machine is named after: it steers your ramp shots into whichever dock is empty, so the multiball setup is about repeating one shot rather than aiming at two different ones. Multiball is the fun part. The points, however, are somewhere else entirely.
The layout

Two flippers, no inlanes at all, and a kickback on the left outlane that is your only ball save. A habitrail carries the plunge to a mini playfield with three lanes marked 1-2-3; three more lanes underneath it spell U-S-A. There is a seven-target SHUTTLE bank down the left wall, a seven-target STATION set split between a centre bank of three and a right bank of four, a three-drop bonus bank, a drop target guarding the ramp, two poppers, and a single standup on the right wall that most players walk past.
Docking and multiball

Get one ball into each dock and multiball is armed. The ramp off the left flipper is the shot, and the Space Station diverter does the aiming for you. If you use the centre popper instead, the game holds your ball there, rotates the station, and only then pops it — so it always lands in the empty side. Once both docks are full, stop ramping: a third ramp shot ejects a docked ball and swaps yours in for it, undoing the setup. Either popper starts multiball, and the right popper is the easier of the two. A right flipper shot that sweeps the three drop targets often carries straight into it, doing two jobs at once.

Re-dock two balls during multiball and you collect the Rescue Jackpot. It takes two ramp shots, which is exactly why the jackpot rarely grows large — it starts at 200,000 and only creeps up by 10,000 each time a multiball ends without it. Afterwards, remember that you cannot dock at all until you have completed the 1-2-3 lanes again. Until you do, every ball you send at a dock is ejected the moment it arrives.
Where the points actually are

Stop 'N' Score is the scoring mode, and it lives behind the drop target in front of the ramp. Knock it down and a number starts cycling between 20,000 and 99,000 for around 25 seconds. Whatever it reads when your ramp shot registers is what you are paid — multiplied by the Stop 'N' Score multiplier. That multiplier is built in the U-S-A lanes, one level per completion, up to 5x.

So the route to a big game is patience rather than reflexes. Build U-S-A to 5x before you start the mode. Then cradle, watch the display, and release so the ball trips the ramp switch as the count nears 99,000. Starting Stop 'N' Score at 1x wastes the whole thing; a well-timed shot at 5x dwarfs anything else on the machine, multiball included.
The banks, and the target nobody hits

SHUTTLE and STATION each pay one award, drawn at random at the start of every ball and displayed on lamp banks in the middle of the playfield. The pool is the same for both: Special, extra ball, 50,000 with the kickback relit, 50,000 with a bonus ball, 150,000 with hold bonus, 75,000, or a plain 25,000. Check what you are playing for before you commit to seven targets.

And here is the rule most players miss. The single standup on the right wall is not decoration — it re-randomises whichever of the two awards it is currently lit for. Drawing 25,000 at the start of a ball is not a sentence you have to serve. Keep hitting it and fish for the extra ball or the Special. Once you have completed U-S-A four times, the same target also carries a Special of its own, so it earns its keep twice.
Small things worth knowing

items: The jet bumpers open at a nearly worthless 500 a hit and climb 500 per 1-2-3 completion to a 3,000 ceiling. That value carries between balls by factory setting.
The three-drop bank raises your end-of-ball bonus multiplier to a maximum of 7x. Reaching 4x lights the extra ball, and clearing the bank once more is what actually awards it.
The right outlane pays 100,000 when lit — the only outlane on this machine that scores anything.
The kickback is your single save and nothing relights it except the 50,000-plus-kickback award from the two banks. By factory setting it starts lit on each ball, but an operator can switch that off.

**The bonus ball** is the sleeper award. It is a timed ball at the end of the game — 25 seconds by default, 45 if you reached multiball at any point — and draining does not end it. The ball is returned to the plunger until the clock runs out.

body.text: That last one is worth planning for. Because drains cost you nothing during the bonus ball, it is the one stretch of this game where you should take shots you would never otherwise risk. Go straight at the ramp, start Stop 'N' Score, and shoot for the top of the number. It is also a second reason to reach multiball even on a poor game: it nearly doubles the bonus ball.

name: Spider-Man
description: How to play Stern's Spider-Man: the two skill shots, white arrows and shot multipliers, the four villain battle ladders, Black Suit Multiball, Spider Sense and Battle Royale.

body.text: Spider-Man is one of Steve Ritchie's fastest layouts and one of the most welcoming rulesets Stern has shipped. A beginner can flail at it and still start battles; an expert can stack four things at once. The structure is unusually clean — four villains, three levels each, a reward at the end of every wave. Learn which shot feeds which villain and you get to choose what your game looks like.
Two skill shots, and one of them matters more

The standard skill shot is a full plunge into the flashing WEB lane. It pays 250k rising by 25k, doubles the pop bumpers for the ball, and — the part people miss — adds **five** to your bonus multiplier. The super skill shot is a soft plunge that dies on the upper right flipper, followed by the side ramp: 500k rising by 50k, plus 100k on the Venom Value and progress toward a Venom battle. On ball three the standard skill shot doubles your end-of-ball bonus and the super triples it, once each per game. The save after a super skill shot is very short.
The three waves

Four villains, each with three battles. Beating all four once lights the extra ball at the left orbit; twice lights both orbits for Battle Royale; three times lights the Light Lock target for a Special. That ladder is the spine of the game.

items: **Sandman** — clear the moving three-bank, then hit the inner standups and the figure. Sandman himself scores double, in points and in damage. Finish in the centre hole.
**Doc Ock** — shots to the right saucer lower the figure. All three of his battles are multiballs, and they stack with Black Suit Multiball in either order.
**Green Goblin** — hit all five left-wall standups, then one more to start. Then keep hitting the flashing ones: six, eight, twelve hits for the three levels.
**Venom** — everything runs through the side ramp, which means everything runs through the upper right flipper. The left ramp helps in early battles but never qualifies one.
Battles stack freely. The only limit is that progress toward the next Doc Ock battle pauses while one is running.

body.text: White arrows and shot multipliers

Six major shots carry white spider arrows: both orbits, all three ramps and Doc Ock. Sweep the set and every arrow starts strobing — the very next shot you make gets a **2x multiplier for the rest of the ball**. This is a decision, not an accident, so pick deliberately. Putting it on the side ramp is enormous, because the third Venom battle is eight side ramp shots and the biggest Black Suit Supers are there too. Completing the arrows also lights both orbits to start one of five forty-second timed modes, and finishing that mode upgrades your multiplied shot from 2x to 3x.
Black Suit Multiball

Hit the Light Lock target until the locks light at the orbits, then shoot a green-lit orbit three times. Two jackpots sit at each major shot, twelve in total. The jackpot value starts at 250k on ball one and grows 500 points per pop bumper hit across the whole game, not per ball, which is why feeding the pops is never wasted time here. Clear all twelve and Super Jackpot pairs light: two at the left ramp at four times value, two at the side ramp at eight. Anything you start before or alongside your third lock comes into the multiball with you.
Spider Sense is your add-a-ball

Completing the three Spider Sense standups arms the lane behind them with an award tied to whatever you have running — mode time, added value, or an add-a-ball during multiball. Awards stack and stay lit until collected or until the ball ends, and one trip through the lane takes everything. The detail that matters is ordering: awards are assigned to your active modes oldest first, so if you started Green Goblin and then a Doc Ock multiball, the first completion arms a Green Goblin award and you need a **second** completion before the add-a-ball appears. The lane sits behind the upper right flipper and only opens with that flipper raised.
Venom Value, and why the spinner matters

Two of the three Venom battles pay a running number called the Venom Value on every shot. It starts at 250k, caps at 750k, and holds from ball to ball. Every spinner rotation adds 1,250, every super skill shot 100k, every completed Venom battle 25k. A plain side ramp shot collects it any time. Building it early turns the eight-shot third battle from a chore into a scoring round — especially with a 3x multiplier on that ramp.
Battle Royale

The reward for the second wave, and the best scoring in the game. Every shot is lit at 250k, the four villain shots pay 750k the first time each, and everything you collect is added into a Royale Jackpot waiting at the right ramp. Completing every red spider shot adds another 1,500,000. Round one pays at least 3,250,000, and cashing it advances the round and adds a ball for the first two. Grind the left orbit to pad the jackpot first. From round three Venom must be shot via the side ramp. One last kindness: when Battle Royale is ready both outlanes flash, and a drain is replunged as a Last Chance.

name: Stargate
description: A player's guide to Gottlieb's Stargate: the Sarcophagus skill shot, Quartz trading, the seven Segments, the six modes, and both wizard multiballs.

body.text: Stargate is a late Gottlieb with more going on than its reputation suggests. There are six modes, four multiballs, a currency you collect and trade, a drop target ladder worth a hundred and fifty five million, and two separate wizard modes. It also has Gottlieb's catch-all flippers, which hold almost anything that comes back at them — and that fact is what makes several of its modes farmable.
The layout

items: **Sarcophagus** — a gate in the left outlane that swallows the ball into a space under the apron and returns it on its own schedule. Not a normal kickback.
**Pyramid** — the gold centrepiece. A very narrow entrance, and where every mode starts.
**Guardians** — two raising figures protecting the left lane and the Trade Quartz kicker. Each has a standup at its base.
**Transporter** — a hidden kicker at the end of the left lane, holding a rotating pool of awards.
**Trade Quartz** — behind the right Guardian. Adds a Quartz and offers you a trade you accept with the right flipper or refuse with the left.
**Both ramps** — steep, with narrow sweet spots. The left starts the combo sequence; the right spots STARGATE letters.
**Right lane** — blocked by an oversized drop target the game raises and lowers. The Hurry-Up shot.
**Drop targets** — a three-bank on the lower left and a two-bank halfway up, marked five, ten, twenty, forty and eighty million.
**Segment circle** — seven inserts nearest the flippers, one per feature. All seven is the wizard multiball.

body.text: Start every ball at the Sarcophagus

The skill shot is a plunge that carries past the right ramp return intersection and on to the Sarcophagus, worth ten million plus a Sarcophagus award. Too soft and the ball dribbles down the right ramp return; too hard and it leaves through the top hole to the upper flipper for nothing at all. It is worth the practice, because odd-numbered Sarcophagus visits start multiball outright. If you miss and it comes down the right ramp return, catch it and shoot the left lane instead for ten million and a Horus advance. The only other route in is to knock the right lane drop target down and shoot the lane behind it before the window closes — miss that window and the target stays flat, leaving the lane dead.
Quartz and the Super Jackpot

Quartz arrive from Sarcophagus awards, Transporter awards, White Pyramid and STARGATE completions and the middle target of the three-bank. Trade Quartz offers a prize scaled to how many you are holding: small point awards low down, an extra ball around seven to nine, a double Super Jackpot advance in the low teens, and at twenty and above either all seven Segments at once or the Super Jackpot itself. Trading spends everything you hold, so refusing early offers is usually correct. The Super Jackpot starts at a hundred million and holds all game, and it is fed by Transporter awards, that Quartz double advance, STARGATE completions and the fifth combo shot. Build it to something serious before you trigger the wizard modes, because both of them pay in Super Jackpots and neither is worth much on a small one.
The six modes

items: **Battle** — both Guardians up and their shots pay the Horus bonus. Twenty seconds to start, three more per shot, and the shots feed each other. Easily the best mode here.
**Ra's Temple** — two Ra target hits add two balls, then the Pyramid pays fifty million per shot with no cap.
**Quartz** — both ramps strobe and each adds a Quartz. Simple and farmable with two balls under control.
**Rebellion** — pop bumpers worth five million each. Park a ball and keep feeding the nest.
