Nudge right as the ball enters the outlane to catch the post.

Start all twelve modes — starting, not completing — and the saucer lights for **Eternal Life Multiball**: six balls, roughly thirty seconds, every switch except the outlanes worth 10M, and a billion for sweeping the lot. That is the reason mode selection with the ramps is the skill that actually separates good games from great ones here.

name: Freddy: A Nightmare on Elm Street
description: How Freddy's awake-and-asleep loop works: earning items before a nightmare, filling the Freddy Meter, spending kruegerands, and reaching Dream Warriors and the Final Nightmare.

body.text: Freddy runs on one idea almost nothing else in pinball copies: you are either awake or asleep, and the two states play completely differently. Awake is ordinary pinball, where you gather items, currency and saves. Asleep is a nightmare, where you fight Freddy on a clock. Players who do well treat the awake state as preparation, not filler — what you are holding when you fall asleep decides whether the nightmare is winnable.
Falling asleep, and what happens next

Three things put you under: the plunger skill shot, the 1... 2... mystery award from the boiler room, and simply running out of time on the sleep meter. Once you are in a nightmare, every flashing FREDDY shot advances the Freddy Meter billboard by two places. Fill it and the boiler room qualifies; shoot the boiler and Freddy goes down for 10,000,000 times the number of the nightmare you are in. If multiball is still running when he falls, you do not wake up — the jackpots light instead.

There are seven nightmares in the ladder, each opening with its own mix of multiball, lit Save Soul targets and an active Freddy jackpot. The first time you see one the game is generous, handing over free items and a partly filled meter. Play it again and none of that help arrives.
The three items

items: **Multiball** — the nightmare opens with multiball already running, which means more flashing shots per second and a much faster meter.
**More power** — every Freddy shot advances the meter three places instead of two.
**Set alarm** — the boiler room qualifies five seconds before the nightmare ends. Grab him there and the nightmare carries on into the awake state, which is the best position in the game.

body.text: The sleep meter is a vertical billboard in the upper centre of the playfield, and it works both ways. Time drives it down toward asleep; coffee shots drive it up. Push it all the way to the top and you become Fully Awake, which does two things: the captive ball starts strobing, and two otherwise unreachable awards come online. Hit the centre left spot target while fully awake for **Hidden Mode**, a multiball where every boiler room shot pays a flat 10,000,000 — you get one per player, per game. Hit the captive ball spot target instead for **Freddy's Bones**, which hands you all three next-nightmare items at once, or twenty kruegerands if you already have them.
Kruegerands and the shop

Kruegerands are currency and worth hoarding — anything unspent is collected at the end of the game, and each is worth a million points in the Final Nightmare. To spend them, roll the right return lane while lit, which flashes Freddy's head for exactly one shot; the head is reached by shooting up through the pop bumpers. What is on the shelf depends purely on how many you carry: 10 to 19 buys ten souls, 20 to 29 buys Kruegerand Multiball, 30 to 39 a hurry-up extra ball, 40 to 49 a straight extra ball, and fifty or more buys Dream Warriors outright. Shopping early is usually a mistake.
Jackpots, combos and Dream Warriors

Defeat Freddy during multiball and five jackpot lamps flash. Each shot collects one and puts that lamp out, and when only one is left it relocates to the captive ball and stays active there — so the end of a jackpot round is a shot you can repeat. Separately, the combo feature is a three-part chain: roll the left return lane to qualify the captive ball, hit the spot target in front of it while lit, and that opens the top left gate and briefly flashes the centre jackpot. The window is short, so plan the third shot before you take the second.

Those two plus a Freddy jackpot are what Dream Warriors needs: one multiball jackpot lamp, one Freddy jackpot lamp, one combo jackpot lamp, and the lower left kicker qualifies. Inside it, the strobing shot pays a super jackpot then jumps elsewhere — until it lands on the upper left spot target, where it stops moving and stays live as long as you hold multiball together.
Saves, points and the endgame

items: **Take That** (top left target) changes with how long games have been lasting on the machine. Under three minutes it gives kick save, then claw save, then a hurry-up extra ball, then 20,000,000. Over three minutes it pays 5,000,000, then 10,000,000, then a hurry-up extra ball.
**The claw** between the flippers comes from completing C-L-A-W and catches balls the flippers cannot. Using it resets the letters.
**Pop bumpers** add 300,000 to your end-of-ball bonus per hit, or a full 1,000,000 each when flashing — bumper time is not wasted time here.
**The T.V. Set** pays 10,000,000 multiplied by consecutive hits while it flashes out, so set up a repeat rather than taking one and leaving.
**Low game special** — start your last ball under 20,000,000 and the right outlane lights for a special.

body.text: The Final Nightmare always opens as a four-ball multiball. Complete five strobing shots to qualify the boiler room, then finish him there; if multiball ends first, the game gives you a grace period rather than cutting you off. The payout is why you hoard all game — a million per soul, a million per kruegerand, and ten million for each Freddy you have already put down.

name: Super Mario Bros.
description: A guide to Gottlieb's Super Mario Bros. pinball: becoming Super Mario, the shell-and-key round cycle, all six rounds, multiball, video mode and destroying seven castles.

body.text: Gottlieb's Super Mario Bros. is a busier machine than it first looks. Count what you are working with: three flippers, the extra one perched on a platform above the main playfield; four sinkholes; two ramps; a loop that returns the ball to the bumpers; and a revolving blue castle in the top right corner. The stated goal is to rescue the princess by destroying seven castles, and the game does something almost no other machine does: **destroyed castles carry over between games**, so a well-played machine may only need one more.
Becoming Super Mario

Every serious decision on this playfield routes through one question: are you Super? Advance S-U-P-E-R at the right ramp while it is lit, or at the left and right holes while they flash. Then hit the left ramp standup target while it is flashing **fast** — a slow flash on that target is worth 5M, a fast flash turns you Super.

Being Super changes four things at once. Round awards double, and that includes extra balls. The right ramp goes from 100K to 500K. Multiball becomes three balls instead of two. And the castle flashes for destruction, which is the only way to knock one down. Protect the state — once the kick save on the left outlane has been used, draining down that lane knocks you back to ordinary Mario.
Shells, then the key

Rounds are the mode structure, and every one costs the same two things. Light three turtle shells by hitting spot targets or ramps that have shells lit, then collect the key by dropping the ball into one of the three holes with the key lamp lit. The bumpers and slingshots toggle which shots carry shells, so outside a round you actively want the ball rattling around the middle rather than trapped up.
Once you have the key the machine offers two rounds at random and gives you about two seconds to pick with the flippers. Hesitate and it takes the left flipper option for you. Six rounds exist:

items: **Bomb** — light the fuse at the flashing left ramp target, then any hole pays 30M, and the upper playfield hole stays lit at 20M for the rest of the ball. That residue is the real prize.
**Yoshi's Countdown** — a single shot to the Yoshi target, opening at 24M and falling. The countdown freezes during multiball.
**Luigi's Cave Count-Up** — the mirror image, climbing to a 48M ceiling before you collect from the cave targets.
**Castle Extra Ball** — one shot into the castle for an extra ball, or two if you are Super when it starts.
**Exclamation** — the best scoring round on the machine, walking up 1M, 2M, 3M, 5M and 10M as you keep hitting the marked targets.
**Mega Bumper** — every pop bumper is worth a million, so stop aiming and keep the ball alive in the middle.

body.text: Multiball

Light 1-2-3-4 in order and then drop into the left hole. The sequence runs left ramp, then the Yoshi target up on the platform, then the right loop that dumps the ball out among the bumpers, and finally the right ramp taken from the upper flipper. Plan two and four together — if you get up to the platform for the Yoshi target, the right ramp is right there.
Two balls normally, three if you are Super. The objective is simply to get balls into the castle, and each one is a jackpot: 5M, then 10M, then 20M, then 40M.
The parts people miss

**Quick Shot** is the cheapest extra ball on the machine and almost nobody chases it. Roll the right inlane and the left ramp starts flashing; hitting it collects from a ladder of 1M, 2M, 5M, 7M, an **extra ball**, then 10M.

**Yoshi bonus** is a slow burn worth knowing about. Every Yoshi target hit adds 500K to a total that is paid when you drain and carries into your next ball rather than resetting. Two hits in a row outside a round lights the target for three million on the next one, and a Yoshi hit also briefly flashes the feather target for 5M.

**Bonus Chance** is a three-reel gamble at the left hole, lit by the cave targets outside a round. Most results are small — 200K for nothing, a million or two for cherries or mushrooms, 5M for any three of a kind. Three sevens pays two hundred million. The mystery award at the right hole, lit by the rollover under the right plastic ramp, can hand you three bonus chances at once, along with extra shells, extra balls or an instant Super Mario.
Video mode, and the trick inside it

Four bullet lamps sit in front of the castle and each roll of the left inlane lights one. Fill them and the next castle shot drops you into a side-scrolling run where the right flipper jumps and the left flipper sprints. Finish it and you get 10M — but **pin the left flipper down for the whole run: at a sprint rather than a walk, Mario is worth 30M at the finish line**.

The same trick has a second life. Once your final castle has fallen and that ball drains, a brief cut-scene sends Mario at the castle; time a jump during it and the payout is 30M rather than 10M again. Finish all six rounds in one game, meanwhile, and the castle flashes for special — briefly, so be ready for it.

name: Bronco
description: Bronco pinball rules: an electro-mechanical wedgehead — plunge for lanes, clear the drop targets, work the bonus ladder and light the special.

body.text: Bronco is a 1977 Gottlieb wedgehead, and it plays nothing like a modern machine. There are no modes, no multiball and no wizard round. What there is instead is a small number of scoring systems that all feed one another, and a game that rewards knowing which of them is worth your attention on any given ball.
The plunge is a real decision

The plunger lane empties into the top arch directly above the A, B and C lanes, so how hard you pull decides which lane the ball drops into. A lit letter is one you have not collected yet. That makes the opening shot the cheapest progress on the machine — on an electro-mechanical game where nothing is guaranteed once the ball is live, a deliberate plunge is worth more than it looks.
What actually scores

items: **A-B-C lanes** — complete the set for the advance. The plunge is the most reliable way to pick up the one you are missing.
**Drop targets** — clearing the bank is the main body of work in a ball and feeds the rest of the scoring.
**Spot targets and saucers** — these hand you progress you did not have to earn cleanly, which matters on a game with no ball save of any kind.
**Kickouts** — learn where each one returns the ball. On a machine this old the kickout angle is the difference between a controlled next shot and a straight drain.

body.text: The alternating relay

This is the part players raised on modern machines miss entirely. Several awards on Bronco alternate between positions rather than staying where you last saw them — the game flips a relay, and the value moves to the other side. If you shoot where the award was last ball rather than where it is now, you are shooting at nothing. Check the lamps before you commit.
Bonus, extra ball and special

The bonus ladder is where a good ball turns into a good game. Run it up through the ball rather than treating it as an afterthought, because on an electro-mechanical layout the end-of-ball collect is a meaningful share of your score.

The extra ball and the special are both lit rather than awarded outright, and both are worth reorganising a ball around. On a five-cent-a-play era machine the special is the whole point — everything else on the playfield is a route toward lighting it.
Order of play

The practical route is: take the plunge letter, clear what you can of the drop targets while the ball is fresh and fast, use the spot targets and saucers to fill in whatever the flippers could not reach, and keep an eye on the relay so you always know which side is currently live. Build the bonus continuously rather than chasing it at the end.

And accept the era. There is no ball save, the outlanes are unkind, and a good Bronco game is often a short one played well rather than a long one. That is not a flaw in the machine — it is what the machine is.

name: The Sopranos
description: A rank-climbing mob game built around a central safe toy, five one-at-a-time episodes, three separate multiballs, and a Boss Mode that makes you prove it twice.

body.text: The Sopranos plays like the show's plot: everything runs through favors, territory, and moving up. You start as an Associate and work toward Boss, and almost every shot feeds that climb. Learn the rank system first and the rest of the game — the safe, the episodes, the three multiballs — makes more sense, since most of it either builds toward a rank or gets doubled by one.
Climbing The Ranks

Four envelope inserts sit at the left loop, right loop, left ramp, and right ramp. Light all four and the **inner loop** turns into an Advance Rank shot worth 500K the first time, +100K every rank after. The other route up is the **safe** — crack it open, close it at the saucer behind it, and that also bumps your rank. Either path works, so lean on whichever side is running hot that ball.

Every rank comes with its own scoring doubler that lasts for the rest of the ball you earn it on — Double Shakedown, Double Safe, Double Truck Heist, an extra ball, Double Meadowlands, and Double Episode scoring, in order. Reach Underboss and you don't just get a doubler — you unlock the Underboss multiball outright. That's as far as the normal ladder goes; Boss is a separate, much bigger ask.
The Safe And The Grind

The safe is the machine's centerpiece, and it's a slow build on purpose. It takes three hits to crack the first time and one more than that every time after, so the crack gets harder to earn even as the payout climbs. Once it's cracked, a saucer opens behind it — drop the ball in there to close the safe back up, bank the bigger award, and advance your rank at the same time.

Running quietly underneath everything else is **Shake Down**, a background counter on the pop bumpers. Every bumper hit chips away at a target that starts at 25 and grows by 5 each time you clear it, and each individual hit pays more as the game goes on too — not a shot you aim for on purpose so much as a reason not to mind a bad carom into the pops. The **spinner** in front of the inner loop works the same way in miniature: it climbs the more you spin it and resets if left alone too long, so a fast inner loop shot is worth chasing on its own.
Five Episodes, One At A Time

Spell SOPRANOS — spin the spinner or hit either stand-up target — and the inner loop lights to start an episode. Only one runs at a time, each on a 30-second clock, and parking in the pop bumpers pauses whichever one is live. Each has its own shape:

items: **Arson** — four flickering shots in any order, 500K to 1.25M, then a 2.5M finish at the inner loop for 6.25M total.
**Exterminate** — a single lit arrow walks you through all four outer shots in sequence, then the inner loop closes it for 3M total.
**Horse Race** — all five arrows go live at once; how many you clear before time runs out decides a payout from 250K up to 4M.
**Executive Game** — a video-mode poker hand played on the flippers: fold and walk away, or bet 140K and see where the cards go.
**Satisfaction** — the same five arrows stay lit with no fixed order, so you can lean on your best shot for a 5.25M episode.

body.text: Three Ways To Multiball

**Stugots Multiball** starts by knocking down the drop target guarding the Stugots and locking two balls there; jackpots build from the drop target before escalating into a double and then a 3.225M super on the Stugots itself. **Bing Multiball** takes three left ramp shots to open a 30-second switch-hitting sprint — clear the target and multiball starts immediately, every shot paying a jackpot up to a 250K cap. **Underboss Multiball** only opens once you've reached that rank: spell UNDERBOSS across the arrows and the safe, then lock up to three balls for a payout that triples, then quintuples. Watch the loops here — a ball shot up either one comes back down the opposite side instead of dropping into the bumpers like everywhere else.

Two mystery awards round out the scoring. The **Fish** saucer on the far left, lit through any inlane or outlane, hands you something matching your progress — an envelope, a rank spot, extra episode time, or an extra ball during multiball. The **Pork Store**, lit from two stand-ups under the right loop and collected at the inner loop, is a wider grab bag that can advance almost any system — and very rarely hands you a jolt of points plus a frenzy where every switch pays out.
Becoming The Boss

Boss Mode doesn't light until you've cleared a full checklist: all five episodes played, Bing Multiball played, four Truck Heists collected, Food Fight cleared, the safe opened, every backpanel character buried, a Super Jackpot banked, Meadowlands run to Trap four times, and Underboss Multiball played. Light it at the inner loop and you get four balls, a long ball saver, and the same eight tasks in the same fixed order all over again. Clear it and the game just resets and asks for another lap — nobody stays Boss for long, so treat one clean run through the checklist as the win.

name: Star Trek: The Next Generation
description: A warp-factor ladder, seven playable missions, three Neutral Zone multiballs, and a Borg battle royale make this one of the deepest rule sets ever put on a playfield.

body.text: Star Trek: The Next Generation throws more at you than almost any machine of its era, but nearly all of it funnels through one system: warp factor. Advance it with the spinner and left ramp and you unlock a new toy at every step — bumper values, held multipliers, a countdown hurry-up, double spinner scoring, and a frantic bonus round at warp 9. Chase warp first and the rest — missions, multiball, ranks, artifacts — starts connecting.
The Picard Maneuver

If you learn one shot on this machine, make it this one. Rip the **spinner** shot on the left orbit, then follow through immediately to the **left ramp** before the ball settles — that's the Picard Maneuver, worth building real muscle memory around. It advances warp faster than either shot alone, awards a triple jackpot during multiball, and turns Q's Challenge into the highest-scoring mode in the game when you chain it over and over.
Warp Factor And Factor Nine

Every ball starts at Warp 1. Warp 2 is a throwaway 5M, but Warp 3 sets the bumpers to a million a pop, Warp 4 lights the spinner for real scoring, Warp 5 holds your bonus multiplier, Warp 6 unlocks Hurry Up and Super Spinner, Warp 7 doubles the spinner outright, and Warp 8 pays an extra ball the first time you see it. Reach Warp 9 and the game drops you into **Factor Nine Mode** — the spinner and left ramp push you through 9.1 onward to 9.9 in tenths, each paying more, on a clock that never pauses. A fresh ball resets you to Warp 1, and the left ramp no longer counts toward warp — only the spinner still does.
Seven Missions To The Final Frontier

**Start Mission** launches whatever's flashing; **Command Decision**, the small hole by the left ramp, lets you cherry-pick instead. Clear all seven and the eighth, **Final Frontier**, lights as the actual finish line of the game. Each plays completely differently:

items: **Time Rift** — every shot pays 10M on a 20-second clock; the two red targets buy more time and, for the first three hits, more money too.
**Worm Hole** — build value on the right ramp and spinner, then cash out on the left ramp before time runs out.
**Search the Galaxy** — hit the three quadrant ramps in the order called out, then finish at the Neutral Zone for the mission's biggest payout.
**Battle Simulation** — load a cannon at any hole and fire when ready; each successful shot climbs a level worth ten times its number in millions.
**Q's Challenge** — no round timer, just a short fuse on each lit shot. This is where the Picard Maneuver turns into a scoring monster.
**Rescue** — thirty seconds to load and save fifty people, using anything that closes a switch to fill the shuttle.
**Asteroid Threat** — freeze a countdown at Start Mission, then clean up all seven shots in a fresh thirty-second sprint.

body.text: Nearly every mission can hand you an **Artifact** too — hit enough of a specific shot and the game tells you. Collect full sets of all four types and Final Frontier pays in the billions: roughly 100M per Artifact just for starting, then every shot scales with how many you're carrying. Show up with none and each shot is a flat 10M instead, so stockpile a few first.
Three Ways The Neutral Zone Turns Ugly

Hit the **Neutral Zone**'s three targets to arm it, then hit it again to pick your poison. **Ferengi** is the friendliest — it stacks up to four balls in play with jackpots at Start Mission worth 10M times however many balls are live. **Cardassian** is tighter: a 2-ball fight where the jackpot falls as your shields do, so rebuilding shields on the spinner matters as much as the jackpot shot itself. **Romulan** isn't a multiball at all — it's a race to cloak three ships, one each on the spinner, left ramp and right ramp, before their timers expire and relight them. None of the three are required for anything else, but Ferengi is worth grabbing just to pad time on the Warp and Time Rift shots you're already chasing.
Multiball, Holodeck, And The Rest

The real multiball is the **Enterprise against the Borg** — lock three balls through the right orbit and left ramp, work the loaded cannon into Start Mission before the third lock for a fatter base jackpot, then chase single, double and triple jackpots while working the spinner to hold your shields up. Let shields hit zero and the jackpot goes dark until raised again. Separately, **Holodeck** lights from repeated right ramp shots and offers a choice: a flat 25M, or **Shuttle Simulation**, a hard video mode steered on the flippers with an Artifact and an extra ball hidden in its later caverns. Watch for **Advance Rank** too — clearing the lanes above the bumpers lights it at Command Decision, and once you're Captain, a lit Advance Rank pays a flat 100M on the spot instead of waiting for bonus.

One more thing worth knowing: when Holodeck reads "Ready" for the third time, pulling the trigger instead of shooting drops you into a hidden **Secret Mission**, a short frenzy where every switch pays out. It won't win the game on its own, but it's a good reminder of how much this ruleset has buried in it.

name: The Simpsons Pinball Party
description: One shared timer ties together seven TV Modes, six major multiballs, and a hidden final wizard mode gated behind clearing all of them.

body.text: There's a lot happening on this table, but almost everything answers to one clock. Every timed system in the game — TV Modes, D'Oh Frenzy, the Treehouse of Horror rounds — shares a single 30-second countdown, and starting or resetting any one of them resets all of them. Learn to keep that timer alive and the rest of the machine stops feeling overwhelming and starts feeling like one long, connected run.
Feed The Timer

**Lite Otto** and the **Krusty Orbit** are the two shots worth memorizing — they're the fastest, most reliable ways to reset the clock back to 30 seconds, and there are at least twenty different triggers across the whole game that do the same thing. The timer pauses the moment the ball lands in the pop bumpers, and the **Pop Target** buys it back: 2 seconds off a bumper bounce, 5 from a clean flipper shot, 10 if you combo it right off the Cletus Orbit. It caps at 60 seconds, and reaching that cap the first time in a game is worth 2.5 million on its own. Keep this shot in your back pocket at all times — you're rarely more than two shots from a full reset.
Double Scoring And Seven TV Modes

Shoot the Krusty Orbit while Otto's window is open and one of ten zones around the table lights for **double scoring** — the bumpers, both orbits, both ramps, both loops, the Garage, and the entire upper playfield. It stacks with everything else running, including TV Modes and multiball, and stays doubled until the timer finally runs dry. Clear all ten zones over the course of a game and Otto turns into the door to something bigger.

**TV Modes** light from the Krusty Orbit and start at the upper playfield's TV Loop — tap the right flipper first to choose which of seven you want. Duffman, Homer's Day, Willie's Woes, Wiggum vs. Snake, Bart's Day, Krusty's Last Stand, and Stop the Monorail each ask for a completely different shot pattern, and each is worth roughly 2.5 million cleared. Finish all seven you've started in one timer run and every major shot on the table turns into a **Victory points** machine — 100K a shot for one completed mode, climbing all the way to 2.5 million a shot if you cleared the full set.
Hurry Ups, Daredevils, And The Rest Of The Main Game

**Comic Book Guy** lights a Hurry Up at one of six major shots, and hitting him again stacks a second one running at the same time — worth real money if you can chain three or more collections together. The **Bully standups** light a **Daredevil Mode**, started at the **Captive Ball**; each of the four types tracks a different family of shots toward 750K, paid out only at the end of the ball, so don't tilt while one's live. Off to the side, the **Cletus Orbit** hands out one of 26 named kids per shot, the **Nuclear Value** builds in the pop bumpers and collects at the Pop Target, and both the **Garage** and **Springfield Elementary** hide genuine grab-bag awards behind repeated shots.

Two real multiballs anchor the base game. **Itchy & Scratchy Multiball** needs the drop target bank cleared, the hole shot, the bank cleared again, then the hole a second time — pick one of four jackpot flavors with the right flipper first. **Couch Multiball** needs three balls locked on the upper playfield, after which eight shots pay Jackpots and the Couch ramp itself pays a Super worth five times the going rate. Collecting five Supers across the game — one for each family member — quietly counts toward something much bigger.
Six Hidden Doors
Nearly every major system in this game hides a secret finale behind full completion, and each is worth hunting down on its own:

items: **Springfield Mystery Spot** — clear all ten double scoring zones, then shoot Otto again. Your flippers swap sides for a five-ball round where everything's worth 500K and doubled.
**Alien Invasion** — finish all seven TV Modes to unlock four escalating phases of locking balls anywhere you can find room.
**Secret Stash** — clear all six Hurry Ups, then hit Comic Book Guy once more for a bonus round built entirely around them.
**Daredevil Mania** — clear all four Daredevil Modes, then hit the Captive Ball for an untimed 5 million point target.
**Scratchy's Revenge** — play through all four Itchy & Scratchy flavors, and the hole starts firing single balls worth chasing on their own.
**Pretzel Multiball** — collect all 26 Cletus Kids for a switch-hitting multiball that's enormous when stacked onto Couch Multiball.

body.text: Clear the first five of those — Mystery Spot, Alien Invasion, Secret Stash, Daredevil Mania, and Scratchy's Revenge — along with five Super Jackpots in Couch Multiball, and any hole shot in single-ball play unlocks the **Super Duper Mega Extreme Wizard Mode**, exactly as dramatically named in-game as it sounds. It's a five-ball round where every shot pays a growing Jackpot, either target bank strobes a 5x Super Jackpot, and locking a ball in the Couch multiplies whatever Super you're chasing for a short window. Getting there takes most of a great game, which is exactly the point — this table rewards depth over speed, and the six doors above are the map for finding all of it.

name: Tales of the Arabian Nights
description: A spinning Lamp toy drives real end-of-ball bonus while seven Tales feed Jewels toward a two-stage Genie Battle finale.

body.text: Everything on this table eventually points back to two things: the Lamp and the Jewels. Spin the Lamp and you're building one of the only real count-up bonuses in modern pinball. Collect Jewels and you're working toward Genie Battle, the two-stage finale where you fight the Genie himself for the Princess's freedom. Almost every other system on the playfield — Harem, the Bazaar, Fireball, Tiger Loops — exists to feed one of those two goals.
The Lamp Is The Game

The **Lamp** sits on a nearly frictionless rotating disc dead center on the playfield, and a solid shot to either post can send it spinning around a dozen times at once. Fourteen blue lights track your spins toward **Lightning Lamp**, a short scoring frenzy that retriggers every 15 spins for the rest of the game, worth 250K or more per hit once it's running. Post angle matters: horizontal posts (like a clock reading 9 and 3) are easy to spin hard and can even send the ball straight into the **Genie** if you split them; vertical posts are nearly impossible to work cleanly and turn into a drain risk instead — leave the Lamp alone when it's sitting that way and go for the standups instead, since they're wide open.

This all matters because of **bonus**. Every Lamp Spin is worth 10,000, every Genie hit 10,000, every Jewel 50,000 — all multiplied by a Bonus X that climbs when you fully hit a lit captive ball, up to 12x. Both the raw count and Bonus X carry across balls, so working the Lamp hard early in a game pays off on every ball after. Done right, the Lamp alone is worth over 14 million in bonus — more than the replay score on most machines.
Multiball, Harem, And The Bazaar

Hit the Genie five times to spell G-E-N-I-E and Lock lights at three spots at once — the Left Orbit, the Right Orbit, and the center Lock lane. Fill two of them and the Genie lights for the start; hit him and his magnet pulls the ball into the playfield to kick off **Multiball**, where spinning the Lamp raises a Jackpot collected right back at the Genie. Separately, **Harem** lights automatically every ball at the Left Orbit — spell H-A-R-E-M there, or catch three lucky bounces out of the Jet Bumpers into the Harem Sneak-In, and **Harem Multiball** begins with every switch paying the Jackpot.

The **Bazaar** scoop spells B-A-Z-A-A-R from its two nearby standups, or from an unlit scoop shot directly, and pays a random award once the word is complete — everything from small points to an outright Extra Ball. The same scoop does double duty for **Make A Wish**: hit it while Make A Wish is lit and choose Jewels on the left flipper or a random award on the right. Take the Jewels almost every time — it can finish a Mode outright without you having to play it at all — unless you're specifically chasing an Extra Ball on Tiger Loops or sitting on a big Bonus X worth cashing in early.
Seven Tales, One Jewel Each

Five **Golden Symbol** lights mark the shots that matter during whichever Tale is running — both standup banks, the Ramp, and both orbits. Tap the left flipper before a ball starts to choose which of the seven is lit, complete whatever it asks, then shoot the Ramp to collect its Jewel. Only one runs at a time, and none are timed, so losing the ball just picks up where you left off next time.

items: **Sinbad and the Rocs** — one Jet Bumper hit lights the Jewel; the rest is just points.
**Ali Baba** — spell S-E-S-A-M-E across both standup banks. Genuinely hard; a fine one to Wish away.
**The Flying Horse** — smash Golden Symbol "statues" hunting for a randomly hidden prize. Also worth Wishing away.
**Scheherazade** — hit any lit Golden Symbol once and you're done.
**The Great Camel Race** — four or five Symbol hits, in any combination, wins it.
**The Flying Carpet** — one Ramp shot lights it, the next one collects it. The easiest Tale by far.
**Cyclops** — hit either captive ball once for the Jewel; it stays live afterward for escalating bonus points.

body.text: Two things are worth hunting for along the way: light one **Shooting Star**, then light the second while Make A Wish is already lit, and the **Ruby** turns your next Wish into two Jewels instead of one. And watch for a weak shot that falls off the Ramp's spiral — it's rewarded with a free Secret Ball Lock, once per game.
Genie Battle

Collect all seven Jewels and the Genie lights for the wizard mode. He takes the Princess and summons Skeletons in her place — every Golden Symbol shot and both captive balls kill one, and after roughly six to eight kills the game locks a ball and serves another. Once locked, the real fight starts: unlimited balls, every shot pulling the Princess toward you while the Genie pulls back on his own, and the Shooting Stars completely disabled, so balls will drain constantly. Launch every ball the instant it's served — leaving one in the plunger lane only speeds up the Genie's pull. Win, and it's a flat 20 million points, the single biggest award anywhere on this table.

name: Creature from the Black Lagoon
description: A drive-in monster movie built on spelling F-I-L-M to unlock a Search-and-Rescue multiball where every Jackpot gets bigger with every Super you collect.

body.text: Creature runs on a simple premise dressed up in a lot of 1950s B-movie charm: spell F-I-L-M, lock a ball, and go rescue the Girl from the Creature in Multiball. Almost everything else on the playfield — the Slide's rotating awards, the Right Ramp count-up, Move Your Car — exists to either help you spell F-I-L-M faster or pad your score while you work toward it. Get comfortable with the letters first and the rest of the machine falls into place.
Spelling F-I-L-M

Each letter has its own shot, and F-I-L-M has to be completed once for every Multiball you want to start. **F** comes from spelling K-I-S-S at the Left Saucer — four hits does it, and a well-timed plunge around the Back Orbit can bank several letters at once as a skill shot. **I** comes from lighting all four **Menu Targets**, which the unlit Snackbar itself will spot for you early in a game. **L** comes from rolling through all four **P-A-I-D** lanes, steered by either flipper, and also nudges your bonus multiplier up a step. **M** comes from the **Slide** — it stays lit for this letter until you collect it, making it the easiest of the four to grab reliably.

Letters pay by the order you collect them, not by which letter they are — 2M, 4M, 6M, then 8M for the fourth — with an extra 8M Sequential Film Bonus if you happened to get them in F-I-L-M order. And there's a real bonus for style: finish K-I-S-S for the F letter, then immediately hit the Slide for M, and you'll bank a 4M Double Film Letter Combo on top of everything else. There's no Triple version, so don't go looking for one.
The Slide, The Right Ramp, And Move Your Car

The **Slide** does more than spell M — every hit after your first cycles through **Mega Menu** (hit all four Menu Targets in 20 seconds for up to 20M), a random **Playground Award** (Jet Bumpers at 1M, Intermission Time, or the excellent **Unlimited Millions**, worth 3M climbing for a full 24 seconds on the Left Ramp), and **Big Millions** (the Right Ramp climbing for a fast 10 seconds). Unlimited Millions in particular is worth planning around — nine straight Left Ramp shots during a good run can pay well over 100M on its own.

Separately, every **Right Ramp** shot counts toward three thresholds outside of multiball: **Snack Attack** at four hits (a countdown collected at the Snackbar), **Video Mode** at eight (punch a Peeping Tom with the flipper buttons — 17 hits in 15 seconds for a knockout), and **Super Scoring** at twelve, which lights nearly everything in the game at once for a wild 20-25 seconds. And don't sleep on **Move Your Car**: five Center Shots start it, then a fast countdown followed by a 15-second window to stack 2x, 3x and 4x follow-up shots for up to 80M total — genuinely one of the best point-for-effort shots on the table.
Multiball

Complete F-I-L-M and lock a ball at either the Left Saucer or the Slide to start it. Three Search targets light — both saucers and the Snackbar — and you have to guess which one is hiding the Girl; it's entirely random which one it turns out to be. Find her for 5M times your Playfield Multiplier, rescue her at the Snackbar for 10M more, then chase the Jackpot there. Somewhere between 10 and 30 **Jet Bumper** hits lights the **Super Jackpot**, worth double the base value — and collecting it permanently doubles that base for the rest of the game.

The real trick to a big Multiball is the **Whirlpool**. Shoot the Left Ramp during multiball and the ball gets diverted onto a long swooping path that dumps it into the Whirlpool, where every revolution spots a letter in CREATURE. Complete the word and your Playfield Multiplier steps up, to a cap of 4x on normal settings — and that multiplier applies to every Jackpot and Super Jackpot you collect afterward. The strongest players trap one ball on a flipper and run the other through the ramp over and over before ever touching a Jackpot shot, since running the multiplier up first turns a 40M Jackpot into something much larger.
Secrets Worth Hunting For

A ball that loops the Back Orbit without ever having been fired from the plunger — the easiest way is a fast Center Shot that carries all the way around — scores a hidden Sneak-In Bonus most players never find. And if you're paying close attention, holding both flippers at exactly the right moment turns up a run of small, genuinely funny secrets: right as the Snackbar's sign flips to "OPEN," right as the attendant hands over a menu award, and right at the "KNOCKOUT" moment of a won Video Mode. None of them are worth much, but they're worth knowing about — this is a game that rewards paying attention to its own jokes almost as much as it rewards good shooting.

name: Wizard of Oz
description: How Wizard of Oz actually works: the four skill shots, Horse of a Different Color, the ramp's two destinations, the Witch, Rescue Multiball, and the eight jewels the wizard mode demands.

body.text: Wizard of Oz was Jersey Jack Pinball's first release, and it plays like a company trying to prove a point: a widebody table stuffed with two upper mini-playfields, a captive Witch toy, and a ruleset that stacks a genuine RPG's worth of side-systems under one long climb toward a single wizard mode. Every shot on the table does at least two jobs. Learning it is less about memorizing one path and more about learning which of eight features you're currently neglecting.
Starting strong

Every ball opens with a choice. The lazy skill shot is a plunge into the flashing Oz lane, worth 5,000 climbing with each one you collect. The better options all share one requirement: feed the ball to the upper right flipper first, then take a real shot with it. From there you can hit the Witch target to bank points and start a hurry-up immediately, hit the standup near the left pop bumpers to launch a Haunted Forest mode on the spot, or — if you clock which letter is flashing on the B-A-L-L bank before you plunge — hit that exact target to spot the whole word at once. None of the three pay off unless the ball reaches that upper flipper clean, so a soft, controlled plunge beats a hard one here.

Once the ball is rolling, keep an eye on the Oz lanes at the very top. They don't do much alone, but every completed O-Z pair adds a full multiple to your end-of-ball bonus, up to 10x, and that bonus adds up fast on a long ball.
The six horses

Horse of a Different Color is Wizard of Oz's quiet scoring engine, and it rewards a very specific kind of greed: sameness. Six shots — the Crystal Ball spinner, left orbit, Castle Entrance kicker, ramp, right orbit, and Throne Room — light for a random colored horse, and landing one adds it to a running stack. Hit the same color again and it just gets more valuable instead of adding a new horse. Once you've built a stack of four to seven horses (the target shifts by one after every payout), the hidden Collect Lane behind a raised right flipper is where you cash in. All matching colors, or all completely different colors, multiplies your total by the horse count; anything in between cuts it in half. Land an all-rainbow set and that multiplier jumps to 5x.
Two roads from the ramp

The ramp is the busiest shot on the table, and where it sends the ball depends on what you've done beforehand. Roll one of the three character lanes — Lion, Tin Man, Scarecrow — scattered around the playfield and follow it immediately with a ramp shot, and you lock that character toward Emerald City Multiball; do that for all three and the multiball starts on its own. Ignore the character lanes, and spelling R-A-I-N-B-O-W on the seven colored standups instead lights the ramp for the Twister mini-playfield, where looping the small orbit ten times spins the house and drops you into a random Munchkin Mode. Both systems run through the same shot, so know which one you're building before you send the ball up.

Once Emerald City Multiball is running, the payoff is in the details: pair a qualified character's rollover with a Throne Room shot to collect that character's gift — a diploma, a medal, a heart — and getting all three earns a jewel toward the wizard mode plus a run of victory laps that climb in value every trip.
The Witch, and rescuing Dorothy

Three hits on the Witch target arm a hurry-up; land two more before it times out and you bank it. Do that three times across a game and the Fireball insert lights — one more Witch hit starts Fireball Frenzy, where you chase a roving blue arrow and avoid the red ones for a climbing jackpot. Ten of those earns a jewel and an extra ball, with more waiting every five jackpots after.

Rescuing Dorothy is the other major thread. Capture her by working the Winged Monkey targets, then send the ball around the right orbit so the Monkey toy can carry the locked ball up to the castle. From there it's a fight on the Witch's Castle mini-playfield: spell R-E-S-C-U-E through direct hits, a Search Orbit shot, or the Rescue Saucer for double credit, and breaking through the castle doors starts Rescue Multiball outright. Once it's running, six shots pay an escalating jackpot before falling to half value, and getting any one to its third hit lights a letter and arms the Super Jackpot at the doors.
Chasing the jewels

Battle the Wicked Witch and Somewhere Over the Rainbow both sit at the top of the ladder, and both demand you've actually played the rest of the machine — Emerald City, Rescue Multiball, a Munchkin Mode, and Fireball Frenzy all have to run once before the Witch target will even start the fight. The full wizard mode wants all eight jewels: everything above, plus fifty Yellow Brick Road advances and a completed run through the five Crystal Ball and five Haunted Forest modes. None of it comes from grinding one shot — it comes from treating Wizard of Oz as eight small games running in parallel, and never letting one of them go stale for too long.

Family Guy packs a surprising amount of interlocking rules into a fairly compact layout — a ramp, a captive mini-playfield, six character shots scattered across the table, and a scoop whose job changes completely depending on what's lit. Almost nothing here stands alone: the same pop bumpers drive two mode rotations, and the same Evil Monkey target feeds two more. Learning the table is mostly learning which shots pull double duty.
The opening moves

Every ball opens with the bottom F-A-R-T target lit for the skill shot: 500K the first time it's collected in a game, climbing 250K with each repeat no matter how many balls that takes. Few players ever find the alternate route — the lane running beneath the mini-playfield is a hidden second skill shot, and taking it instead of the F target doubles whatever the current value is and bumps the next skill shot's starting point up by 250K on top of that.

Outside of any mode, Meg, Chris and Stewie each pay their own climbing value on every hit — 100K to start, with a fixed bump per shot that differs by character. Lois builds a smaller rising total on the spinner. All six main characters also feed the end-of-ball bonus at their own flat rate rather than a shared ladder: Meg's hits are worth the most there, Lois's the least. Clearing the X-X-X bank under Peter pays a rising value of its own, up to 250K, and nudges the bonus multiplier toward a 5x ceiling.
Beer Can and TV modes

Two mode tracks share one control — any pop bumper hit rotates both the flashing Beer Can mode and the flashing TV mode forward. Hit the Beer Can standup enough times, five to start and one more each time after, to cash in whichever mode is lit: Collect Beers pays your running hit total, Giggity Giggity maxes the bumpers outright, Happy Hour doubles every score for 20 seconds, and Remember When opens a countdown Jackpot at a random character, starting at 3M and growing a million with every repeat. The fifth slot is Lard Multiball, a two-ball mode built around six Jackpot shots on a ten-second relight timer, paying a 3M Super Jackpot if all six go out at once.

TV modes work off the Lois spinner: ten spins lights TV at the scoop the first time, five more each time after, up to a cap of thirty. The lit scoop banks 500K and starts whichever 30-second mode is flashing — Good Old Boys climbs 500K to a 1M ceiling per shot, Super Griffins tops out at 6.75M for working all six characters, Chicken Fight turns every switch into a punch until a life bar empties, Sexy Party climbs 300K toward a 750K cap per Stewie hit, and Ipecac Contest pays more per shot per extra character worked in, up to 1M with all four. Finish all five and the scoop stays lit for TV Wizard instead of resetting.
Fart Multiball and Crazy Chris

Clear the F-A-R-T bank three times and Fart Multiball begins with two balls and a short save; every restart after needs one more clear, up to six, and starts with three balls instead. Jackpots are priced by demand rather than a flat number — twenty thousand points for every switch hit a given Jackpot requires — so the tougher ones pay more.

Crazy Chris runs on a different pairing. Chris hits knock the Evil Monkey target down in front of the ramp and raise its value; hitting the dropped Evil Monkey while its light flashes banks that total and, if the light says so, opens a 20-second run where every lit shot pays 200K per Evil Monkey hit landed since that run began, up to a 1M ceiling per shot. Drawing Crazy Chris from the Drunken Clam instead skips that math and pays a flat 400K a shot.
Stewie and the mystery saucer

The Drunken Clam rewards shooting it whenever it's lit — nothing it offers is wasted on something you hold. One trick lights P-I-N-B-A-L-L at the scoop, handing control to Stewie's own mini-playfield. Clear its five characters — Lois needs four hits and pays best per hit, the rest need three to five — and your first completion raises a playfield multiplier that holds for the rest of the ball, capping at 3x (it resets when a new session begins). Finish all five and you drop into Stewie Multiball: each character needs a second completion on the real table, both captive balls spell letters toward add-a-balls, and a maxed-out set lights an Evil Monkey Super Jackpot worth 2M. Hit it twice and the second pays 3M, briefly opening the Clam for a Triple Super Secret Jackpot worth three times that.
Sperm Attack

The finale asks for six achievements spread across the whole game — 5 Evil Monkey Jackpots, 10 lit shots inside one Crazy Chris run, 15 Fart Multiball Jackpots, every Beer Can award, a Stewie Super Jackpot, and 25M or more during TV Wizard — before MULTIBALL lights at the scoop. Once it starts, the mini-playfield spends eighteen seconds building a shared Jackpot, then the Clam and the scoop trade a locked ball for two million a shot, sending you back to build the total higher each time you keep the chain alive. None of the six requirements ask you to play differently than you already would — they reward spreading your game around, not camping one shot all night.

name: Family Guy
description: Family Guy pinball rules: TV modes, Fart and Lard multiballs, Stewie's mini-playfield, the Evil Monkey, and the Sperm Attack finale.

name: Avatar
description: How Avatar actually works: the R-D-A skill shot and shot multipliers, Na'vi Scoring and Multiball, Link and Amp Suit Multiball, the unobtainium outlane trick, and Final Battle.

body.text: Avatar's playfield looks empty compared to its contemporaries, and that's by design: almost everything worth shooting is fanned out across the upper third of the table, feeding six parallel features that all report back to one progress ladder. There's no single correct order to play them in. The game just wants every insert on that ladder lit before it will let you anywhere near the finale, so the real skill is juggling six short-term goals instead of grinding one long one.
Getting rolling

The R-D-A lanes at the top hold the skill shot — the D lane flashes by default, worth 250K on the first ball and climbing after. Those same three lanes matter for the rest of the game too: every full R-D-A completion adds to your bonus multiplier and lights one of seven shot multipliers, 2x at first and then a roving 3x once you've doubled all seven. Below that sit the pop bumpers, which build their own value from 3K up to a 20K cap the longer you can keep the ball bouncing.
Na'vi Scoring and the characters

The N-A-V-I bank on the left is the fastest way into the game's main collection mechanic. Spell the word, shoot the bank again, and Na'vi Scoring opens up six flashing arrows — both orbits, the ramp, the link lane, Eywa, and the seeds targets — each one paying a countdown value and lighting a character on the vertical ladder as you go. The Bond inlanes offer a shortcut: roll through all three and one uncollected character's shot flashes on its own for just a couple of seconds, worth grabbing on reflex if you happen to be lined up for it.

Collect all six characters and the N-A-V-I bank itself changes jobs, flashing for **Na'vi Multiball** instead of Na'vi Scoring. Six jackpots at 150K, four double jackpots at 300K once those are gone, then a Super Jackpot worth the sum of everything — over two million even before any shot multipliers get involved, and it restarts the whole cycle at higher values once collected.
Eywa, Banshee, and the link lock

Eywa's captive ball is worth checking constantly. It lights after a rising number of switch hits and always pays something useful — bonus multiplier bumps, timer extensions, and the game's only source of extra balls, which get collected at the ramp. That same ramp spells out Ride a Banshee (three of its seven letters are given free by default), then turns into a 25-second scoring run in its own right once the word is complete.

The lock lane under Jake's pod is a different kind of commitment. One shot traps a ball there and launches a second into play; hitting the trapped ball free starts Link Multiball, where five shots trade off which is lit for a 250K jackpot (unobtainium always pays double) on the way to a Super Jackpot worth three million or more. Land the re-trapped ball fast enough afterward and that Super doubles before the mode settles into open-ended victory laps.
Amp Suit and Bomber Battle

The motorised three-bank in the middle is the biggest mechanical set piece on the table. Lower it, then land five hits on the battle targets behind — either side target covers the first four, but the fifth has to be the bullseye, which pays two million and launches **Amp Suit Multiball**. From there it's six single jackpots, three doubles, and a Super Jackpot that can climb past sixteen million with the right multipliers running — and a second Super is available right after the first, at values raised again.

Away from all that, shots to either orbit outside of multiball quietly count down toward Bomber Battle, worth an instant 500K just for qualifying before its own 25-second run even starts. The seeds targets above the right outlane work the same simple way: enough hits to qualify, one more to start, then every switch on the table scores for a fast, low-effort frenzy.
The unobtainium trick, and Final Battle

Here's the one genuinely counterintuitive shot on the table: hitting the forward-facing unobtainium target lights an outlane insert for a growing points award, and the only way to collect it is to actually drain that ball down the lit outlane on purpose. Do it to both sides in the same ball and you double the target's own value in the process.

That same mechanic becomes the whole final act. Qualify all six feature-ladder inserts and the unobtainium target kills the flippers, launches all four balls, and opens Final Battle — a round built on switch-hit thresholds where the modest reward is a points jackpot at the target itself, but the real money is in deliberately losing balls down both lit outlanes for ten and fifteen million apiece before cashing in the fully built target, which relaunches everything you just drained and starts the next round even bigger.

name: Tron: Legacy
description: How Tron: Legacy actually works: the three skill shots, the uncalled End of Line combo, the minor features around the edges, Light Cycle/Quorra/Disc Multiball, and the Sea of Simulation and Portal finale.

body.text: Tron: Legacy is a feature-based game dressed up as a combo machine. The real goal is simple — light every insert on the progress ladder running up the middle of the playfield — but the table is fast enough, and generous enough with stacking, that you'll trip several of those features by accident before you've consciously aimed at any of them. Learning Tron is mostly about noticing what you already started.
Starting the ball

A soft plunge bounces off Flynn's divider straight into the scoop for the easiest skill shot, worth 500K and climbing. Two harder options exist if the ball misses that bounce: a shot to the left ramp off the right flipper if it rolls down to the right side, or — hold the left flipper button in before you plunge — a full orbit up to the upper left flipper for a shot at the right ramp. Both of the harder options pay a little less than the scoop, but both also light a Light Cycle insert on top, which the easy option doesn't.

Once the ball is live, keep one thing in mind above everything else: the **End of Line combo**. Land any of the six major shots — both orbits, both ramps, both inner loops — and their arrows flash for a moment, inviting you to one-time the ball into the scoop. Do it, and you collect a value that starts at 500K and never resets on its own, climbing with every combo you build even between collections. The game does nothing to announce this — no callout, no light show, nothing on the display tells you it just happened. It is nonetheless the single most valuable thing you can do on this table, more often than not worth more than whatever mode or multiball happens to be running at the time. The only way to lose it is to drain before you cash it in.
The minor features

Scattered around the rest of the playfield are five smaller systems that mostly just happen to you during a normal game. The T-R-O-N targets strobe between three scoring boosts — Double Scoring, Super Bumpers, Super Spinners — and rolling the Zen lane first turns your next hit on any of them into an instant start, no full bank clear required. Banking a few Zen rolls before you cash one in lets a single follow-up shot chain all three back to back.

Light all three C-L-U lanes across the inlanes and the scoop readies **Terminate Clu**, a 25-second run across four marked shots — left orbit, left inner loop, right orbit, and the scoop itself. The four Z-U-S-E standups spell out a switch-frenzy the moment you complete them, and rolling the Zen lane also starts **Find Flynn**, a roaming arrow that wanders the six major shots until you catch it — worth grabbing early since it's one of the cheapest inserts to light. **Follow Gem** is the odd one out: three shots to the stubborn right inner loop start it, and it only gets more valuable the longer you keep the ball moving there, helped along by either spinner adding time to the clock.
Three multiballs, three different shapes

**Light Cycle** is the quickest to reach — light four of six inserts and the scoop starts it — and it rewards a specific chain: a left ramp jackpot flashes the Quorra insert at the left inner loop for a super, and following that with the right ramp scores a fixed double super on top. **Quorra Multiball** asks for five shots at the left inner loop instead, then pays unlimited jackpots there with a real Super Jackpot waiting at Gem, and the Recognizer bank can add two more balls if you need the extra time.

**Disc Multiball** is the flagship, and it takes longer to reach than the other two combined — clear the Recognizer bank, feed the spinning disc seven times, then work through ten jackpots and three double jackpots across two stages before a Super Jackpot that dwarfs anything else on the table, especially with Double Scoring running the whole way through.
The finale

Get every ladder insert at least flashing and the scoop opens **Sea of Simulation**, a single untimed ball that pays out a lump sum for everything you've already solidly completed and hands you one more shot at whatever's still missing. Get all nine inserts fully solid — whether through Sea of Simulation or the hard way — and the scoop instead opens **The Portal**, a four-ball multiball with twenty-one jackpots spread across the whole table and a Super Jackpot waiting at the end of all of them. Owners of the LE cabinet have one more trick available: spelling D-A-F-T-P-U-N-K on the left ramp, twice, for a hidden extra ball and a bonus multiball that doesn't touch the ladder at all — a nice reward for chasing that one ramp shot as hard as the rest of the table wants you to anyway.

name: AC/DC
description: How AC/DC actually works: the two skill shots, choosing and changing songs, the cannon-fired Song Jackpot, the bell's playfield multiplier risk, stacked multiballs, and the Encore finale.

body.text: The playfield doesn't look complicated: a pair of ramps, a pair of loops, three standup banks, a spinner, a lane feeding the bell, and some bumpers rounding it out. What isn't obvious from the layout is Lyman Sheats's code running underneath Steve Ritchie's design — it wires nearly every one of those ordinary shots to whichever song happens to be playing, so almost nothing on this table scores the same way twice.
Starting the ball

A plunge nearly always lands in the top saucer, which kicks out into the AXE lanes — flip to move the blinking lane and land in it for the easy skill shot. Hold the right flipper as the ball exits the saucer instead, and it drops straight to the flippers for a harder, more valuable option: any major shot from there pays more and hands you two VIP passes instead of one. Passes matter more than they look — in regular play, pressing Fire just spots a hit toward your song's key feature, which is fairly minor, but during multiball it spots one of the five major shots toward an add-a-ball, and that's worth holding onto.
Choosing, and changing, your song

Twelve songs, twelve key shots, and picking one at the start of the game is not cosmetic — it decides which shot pays extra for the rest of the ball, through multiballs and everything else, until you deliberately change it. Hitting the key shot for a song you *aren't* playing lights it on the jukebox in the back of the cabinet; light eight of them and a shot into the top saucer — reachable off the right loop, or free on the plunge at the start of a new ball — offers you the choice to switch. Keeping your current song instead just resets the count back to zero. There is genuinely nothing wrong with picking one song, like Hells Bells or War Machine, and never touching the jukebox all game.
The Song Jackpot

Every point you score in your current song mode is quietly added to a separate running total. Spell F-I-R-E on the inlanes and outlanes three times — one shot is free at the very start of the game — and a lit cannon insert appears above the flippers. Shoot the right ramp to feed it, then press Fire to aim at the blinking AC/DC target. Land it and you bank the whole jackpot, easily worth fifteen or twenty million before any multiplier gets involved; miss, and the value holds while you spell F-I-R-E again for another try. Aiming the cannon at the bell instead, when you have the choice, is the safer play — it builds toward a playfield multiplier rather than risking the drain a target shot invites.

That risk is real. The bell is responsible for every playfield multiplier in the game — three hits light 2X for twenty seconds, three more during 2X light 3X — but it's also the riskiest shot on the layout: come up short and you're almost certainly draining, and even a solid hit doesn't guarantee safety. Build your multiplier before you cash in a big jackpot, not after.
Multiball, stacked

Three multiballs correspond to three playfield features: **Jam** to the ramps, **Album** to the three target banks, and **Tour** to the two loops. All three start the same way — shoot the lit right ramp — and Jam usually lights first anyway — not because it needs fewer shots (fifteen ramps is far more than one bank of targets), but because the ramps are safe, repeatable shots you can backhand and combo all day. Album and Tour share a neat trick: jackpots are named chronologically after AC/DC's albums or tours, and landing one while playing a song that actually belongs to that album or tour pays a full song bonus on top, no reset required.

You can't work toward one multiball while another is running, but you can light two or three ahead of time and start them all together the instant the right ramp comes up, for a Double or Triple Multiball. Twenty jackpots into any of them — fourteen for Album — lights the cannon for a Super Jackpot worth the lump sum of every jackpot you have scored to that point, and Triple Multiball adds its own bonus jackpot at the bell once you've landed one of each type.
Hidden depths, and the encore

Premium and LE cabinets hide a second playfield underneath the first. Any song with "Hell" in its name — Hells Bells, Highway to Hell, Hell Ain't a Bad Place to Be — drops you down there the first time you make that song's key shot. It's a minor detour, not a second game, but it's easy to miss if you don't know to look for it.

The real finale is **Encore**, unlocked only after completing all twelve songs — changing away from a song completes it, whether or not you ever shot its key feature — and choosing to change one final time. Three balls walk you back through the shot sequence of your entire game, song by song, re-scoring each one as you land it. It's built to reward finishing the achievement, not to compete for high score, so don't feel obligated to chase it if you're just trying to put up a number.

name: Harry Potter
description: Harry Potter pinball rules: lessons and O.W.L.s, Quidditch deck multiball, horcrux hunting, and the twin wizard modes Deathly Hallows and Battle of Hogwarts.

body.text: Jersey Jack's Harry Potter turns seven school years into a pinball curriculum: attend lessons, win Quidditch, collect allies, and hunt horcruxes toward two separate wizard finales. The layout runs two main flippers plus an upper-right flipper, a left ramp, center ramp, library ramp, right orbit, a Death Eater drop-target hole on the mid-left, wand-lock scoop, and the star piece — a Quidditch upper deck with its own mini flipper, spinner, and standups, reached from the center ramp. Tucked under the upper-right flipper is a sneaky hole shot that even the game's own programmer whiffs on camera.
Core loops

Lessons drive everything: each school year offers a set of class shots, and finishing five in a term lights O.W.L.s — ten total lessons brings the O.W.L.s multiball. Explore Hogwarts multiball builds from banner shots (the green and yellow pairs start pre-spotted, so your first qualification can take as little as two good shots at the center ramp). Quidditch World Cup multiball lives up on the deck: climb the center ramp, work the spinner and standups with the deck's own flipper, and catch the Snitch to cash the round.

The darker half of the game is the horcrux hunt. Wand locks at the scoop stage Golden Trio play, Death Eater raids build danger at the drop target, and each destroyed horcrux marks progress on the seven-piece table. Protego, the outlane save, only lights while a wand lock is already active — plan your risk around it.
Wizard path

Two summits: Deathly Hallows requires earning all three Hallows — no shortcuts — while Battle of Hogwarts asks for any four of the five main multiballs (O.W.L.s counts). Tournament players usually open on the left-ramp skill shot, bank the pre-spotted banners into a fast Explore Hogwarts, and treat the under-flipper hole as a set-up shot from a cradle, never on the fly.

name: Sonic the Hedgehog
description: Sonic the Hedgehog pinball rules: the seven-zone ladder, Goal Ring boss battles, H-E-R-O lanes, Chaos Emerald six-ball multiball, and ring cash-outs.

body.text: Jersey Jack's Sonic the Hedgehog, a Steve Ritchie design for the hedgehog's 35th anniversary, plays like the games: pick a zone, race its checkpoints, reach the Goal Ring, and knock Eggman out of the sky. Two main flippers plus an upper-left flipper on Eggman's battle deck, a crossing right ramp that returns to the opposite flipper, left and center ramps, orbits, a Bash-Dash captive ball, spring kicker targets that fire the ball back hot, and four H-E-R-O rollover lanes split across the lower guides — H and E on the left, R and O on the right.
Core loops

Seven zones from Green Hill up, selectable with the action button — any incomplete zone, any order. Inside a zone, checkpoint shots light the Goal Ring; completing the level swaps you to a boss battle finished by bashing the Eggmobile. Rings bank as you play and cash out at end-of-ball bonus, so a long ball with heavy ring collection pays twice.

Chaos Emerald multiball is the big one — a six-ball affair once the emeralds line up — with Sonic Heroes multiball built off the H-E-R-O lanes and the Bash-Dash. The Chao target lights orbits for garden play, and the white and pink skill-shot inserts reward a controlled launch from the plunger before the zone race begins.
What to respect

The spring targets fire the ball back with real pace — hit them with a plan, not by accident. One outlane carries a spring kickback, so learn which side forgives you. Super Sonic waits at the top of the insert ladder for players who run the full zone table, with Master Emerald Mission, Casino Night, and Boss Rush inserts marking the rest of the late game.

name: Iron Man
description: Iron Man pinball rules: complete the five objectives for Do or Die, spell MONGER to bash the Iron Monger, climb the Mark ladder, and reach Jericho.

body.text: John Borg's Iron Man is a short, ferocious machine built to end your ball fast and make you love it for trying. The layout is wide open: two flippers under unusually wide outlanes with no ball save, left and right ramps that combo for Bogey, left and right orbits carrying spinners, a center spinner straight up the middle, a bash-toy Iron Monger that rises on a magnet, a fast War Machine shot that kicks the ball back at you, a pair of magnet-guarded Whiplash targets, and two banks of red picture targets that spell IRON MAN. Everything is labeled right on the playfield, so the game is never a puzzle, only a fight.
The five objectives

The heart of the game is five objectives: Iron Man, War Machine, Whiplash, Iron Monger and Drones. Spell the red targets for Iron Man and sweep them again for double scoring; clear the roaming blue drone targets to arm War Machine at its shot; hit the Whiplash targets five times to start its multiball; and spell MONGER on the purple orbit and center shots to raise the toy, then bash its edges. Land all five on a single ball and the center flashes for Do or Die, a fifty million hurry-up on a game where thirty million is already a great score.
Marks and Jericho

The long game is the Mark ladder. Each objective you finish lights the next Mark suit, and reaching Mark six opens Jericho, a shoot-everything finale that pays enormous. The Marks carry across balls, so even a rough ball leaves progress on the board. That is a big part of why the game keeps pulling you back for one more start.
What to respect

Two magnets and two wide outlanes do most of the killing here. The Iron Monger's magnet grabs anything shot dead center, so always hit it on a corner. Whiplash flings the ball back at speed and can drain you through no fault of your own, so have both flippers ready for the return. Nudging is part of playing this game well: settle every fast return before you aim, because there is no ball save to bail you out.
Editions

Iron Man arrived in 2010 and was reissued as a Pro Vault Edition in 2014 with the same layout and rules and a brighter, louder presentation. An earlier Classic edition left off the left-outlane kickback and the playfield magnets, but the shots and objectives are otherwise identical, so the same plan works across every version you are likely to run into.

name: Fallout
description: Fallout pinball rules: pick your character, keep your HP up for quests, spell VAULT to open the vault, upgrade your weapon, and start Deathclaw, Wasteland and Vault Multiball.

body.text: Keith Elwin's Fallout turns a pinball machine into a role-playing game. Before the first launch you pick Lucy, Maximus or The Ghoul, and each one plays differently: Lucy has an easier time in the vaults, Maximus gets more out of his power armor, and The Ghoul shrugs off radiation. The layout gives you left, center and right ramps, a left loop and right orbit, a Pip-Boy shot on the upper left, a mutated upper flipper that feeds a long outer loop, a Nuka-Cola bottle-cap spinner that rises and falls, a single pop bumper, and a Deathclaw bash toy on the right.
HP, quests and legendary weapons

Your HP is the clock. Every main quest runs one second per point of HP, so you eat at the yellow Pip-Boy shot until you have at least fifty, then start the blinking quest at the right scoop. The quests range from two-ball multiballs like Wedding Day and The Kings to shot modes like Radscorpion Attack, Mind Control, NOVAC and Find the Target. Finishing one earns a Legendary Weapon, a perk that lasts the rest of the game.
Into the vault

Spell VAULT at the lit letter shots and Open Vault lights at the center ramp. On Premium and LE machines the ball is held while a real vault door swings open, and you go through to a lower playfield for one of several vault modes. On the Pro, you bash the door and play Find the Lunchbox instead. Lunchboxes alternate between Vault Multiball, a three-ball march of jackpots from left to right, and another Legendary Weapon.
The wasteland economy

Caps, junk and fusion cores drive everything else. Light both Nuka-Cola inlanes, slide the flashing one under the ball with the flipper buttons, and rip the dropped spinner for caps to spend at the Sundries shop. Junk upgrades your weapon for a permanent playfield multiplier and unlocks the next Deathclaw Multiball. The pop bumper charges your fusion core, and holding the action button puts on power armor for timed double scoring. A short press uses your Trusty Companion's ability instead.
Multiballs and danger

Time your Deathclaw bashes to cripple its four limbs and start Deathclaw Multiball. Clear the shooting gallery with the Fat Man launcher (or, on the Pro, the left flipper and the mini-nuke stand-ups) for Wasteland Multiball. Watch the radroach stand-ups: a blinking one is a kill, but a solid one is a radiation pool that cuts your max HP until you drink radaway.
Editions

Fallout comes as a Pro, Premium and Limited Edition. The Premium and LE add the moving vault door with its magnetic lower playfield and the multi-axis Fat Man firing into an upper target gallery. The software is still early, and its wizard modes are shown on the playfield but have not been added to the game yet.
